options: The escape of gas through a tiny hole
The spontaneous mixing of gases by random molecular motion until a uniform mixture forms
mcqs.why: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of gases by random molecular motion until a uniform mixture forms; the spreading of perfume or scent in air is due to diffusion.

mcqs.q: Effusion is:
options: The escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum or lower-pressure region without collisions
mcqs.why: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum or a lower-pressure region without collisions, a different process from diffusion.

mcqs.q: The spreading of perfume or scent in air is due to:
mcqs.why: Perfume molecules mix spontaneously with air by random molecular motion, which is diffusion, the process described by Graham's law.

mcqs.q: Graham's law states that the rates of diffusion or effusion of two gases are related by:
options: rate1 / rate2 = sqrt(M2 / M1) = sqrt(d2 / d1)
mcqs.why: From kinetic theory, molecular speed is proportional to 1 / sqrt(m), so Graham's law gives rate1 / rate2 = sqrt(M2 / M1) = sqrt(d2 / d1).

mcqs.q: By Graham's law, the rate of diffusion of a gas is:
options: Inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, so lighter gases diffuse more rapidly
Directly proportional to its molar mass
mcqs.why: At the same temperature all molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so a lighter molecule must move faster; hence the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass.

mcqs.q: The rate of diffusion of hydrogen (H2, M = 2) compared with helium (He, M = 4) is:
mcqs.why: rate of H2 / rate of He = sqrt(M of He / M of H2) = sqrt(4 / 2) = sqrt(2) = 1.41, about 1.4 times.

mcqs.q: Among CH4, NH3, CO2 and O2, the fastest effusion rate is shown by:
mcqs.why: By Graham's law the lightest gas effuses fastest; methane (CH4, M = 16) is lighter than NH3 (17), O2 (32) and CO2 (44), so CH4 has the fastest effusion rate.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen diffuses through a porous plate at 500 cm per minute at 0 degrees C. The rate of diffusion of oxygen through the same plate is:
mcqs.why: By Graham's law, rate of O2 / rate of H2 = sqrt(M of H2 / M of O2) = sqrt(2/32). Now sqrt(0.0625) = 0.25, so rate of O2 = 500 x 0.25 = 125 cm per minute.

mcqs.q: An unknown gas effuses at 0.279 times the rate of H2. Its molecular mass is:
At the same temperature, all gas molecules have the same average kinetic energy (1/2 m v^2). A lighter molecule therefore:
options: Must move faster to have the same kinetic energy as a heavier one
mcqs.why: Since 1/2 m v^2 is the same for all molecules at a given temperature, a smaller m must be matched by a larger v; this is the kinetic-theory basis of Graham's law.

lessons.title: Liquefaction of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Gases can be liquefied by cooling them below their critical temperature and compressing them. The cooling itself comes from the Joule-Thomson effect: a real gas cools when it expands.

Joule-Thomson Cooling

When a compressed gas expands suddenly into a low-pressure region, it must do work against the attractive forces between its molecules to pull them apart. The energy for this work comes from the kinetic energy of the molecules themselves, so their average speed falls and the temperature drops. This cooling on free expansion is the Joule-Thomson effect. When a real gas is allowed to enter a low pressure (vacuum), its temperature usually drops for the same reason: its molecules must move apart against their mutual attractions, and the work done against these forces comes from the molecules' own kinetic energy. An ideal gas, with no attractions, would show no such cooling.

Linde's Method

Linde's method liquefies gases by repeated Joule-Thomson cooling. The gas is compressed, cooled to remove the heat of compression, and then allowed to expand through a nozzle into a low-pressure region, where it cools further. The cooled gas is passed back over the incoming gas in a heat exchanger, cooling it still more, and the cycle is repeated until the gas reaches its liquefaction temperature and condenses.

Everyday Example

In a factory producing liquid air, one of the pipes carrying dry air at -80 degrees C can be blocked with a white solid. That white solid is carbon dioxide, which freezes out of the air at that temperature.

Weather and Tyre Pressure Projects

Daily weather reports show how atmospheric pressure, temperature and humidity vary together over a week: falling pressure with rising humidity often comes before rain. A tyre gauge reads gauge pressure, commonly in pounds per square inch (psi), bar or kilopascals (kPa). Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure (about 14.7 psi or 1 atm), so a tyre that reads zero on the gauge is still full of air at atmospheric pressure.

mcqs.why: Gases are liquefied by cooling below their critical temperature and compressing; the cooling itself comes from the Joule-Thomson effect, in which a real gas cools when it expands.

The cooling of a real gas when it expands into a low-pressure region
mcqs.why: When a compressed gas expands suddenly into a low-pressure region, its temperature drops; this cooling on free expansion is the Joule-Thomson effect.

mcqs.why: To pull the molecules apart against their mutual attractions takes work, and that work is paid from the kinetic energy of the molecules themselves, so their average speed falls and the temperature drops.

mcqs.why: An ideal gas has no attractions between molecules, so no work is done against attractions on expansion and there is no such cooling; the effect proves real gases have attractions.

mcqs.why: The cooled gas is passed back over the incoming gas in a heat exchanger, cooling it still more before its own expansion, so the temperature falls cycle by cycle until liquefaction.

mcqs.why: Gauge pressure is measured above atmospheric pressure, so a zero gauge reading means the tyre's pressure equals atmospheric pressure; the tyre is still full of air at about 1 atm.

lessons.title: Fourth State of Matter: Plasma
lessons.notes_html:
Besides solid, liquid and gas there is a fourth state of matter: plasma, the state of most of the visible universe.

Definition and Properties

Plasma is a gas in which a large fraction of the atoms are ionised into free electrons and positive ions. It conducts electricity, responds strongly to magnetic fields, and glows when excited. Most of the visible universe is plasma, including the Sun and other stars, lightning, and neon signs.

mcqs.q: Plasma is:
options: A fourth state of matter, a gas in which a large fraction of the atoms are ionised into free electrons and positive ions
mcqs.why: Besides solid, liquid and gas there is a fourth state of matter: plasma, a gas in which a large fraction of the atoms are ionised into free electrons and positive ions.

mcqs.q: Plasma conducts electricity because it contains:
mcqs.why: Plasma is an ionised gas, so its free electrons and positive ions can carry charge; it conducts electricity and responds strongly to magnetic fields.

mcqs.q: Plasma responds strongly to:
mcqs.why: Because plasma consists of charged particles (free electrons and positive ions), it responds strongly to magnetic fields, unlike an ordinary neutral gas.

mcqs.q: When excited, plasma:
mcqs.why: Plasma glows when excited; this is seen in neon signs, where the ionised gas gives out light.

mcqs.why: Plasma is the state of most of the visible universe, including the Sun and other stars, lightning, and neon signs.

lessons.title: Kinetic Molecular Interpretation of Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
Liquids lie between gases and solids: their molecules are close together like a solid, but they can move past one another like a gas. The kinetic molecular theory explains their properties from this in-between state.

Properties of Liquids

On the basis of kinetic molecular theory: (i) Diffusion: liquid molecules are in constant motion and can move from one place to another, so two liquids mix slowly by diffusion. (ii) Compression: liquid molecules are already close together, so liquids are almost incompressible. (iii) Expansion: on heating, molecular motion increases and the molecules move slightly apart, so liquids expand a little. (iv) Motion of molecules: molecules slide over one another but cannot move freely like gas molecules. (v) Intermolecular forces: forces between liquid molecules are strong enough to hold them together but weak enough to let them flow.

Dynamic Equilibrium

Dynamic equilibrium between two physical states means that the two opposite changes go on at the same time and at equal rates, so that the amounts of the two states stay constant although molecules keep changing state. For example, in a closed bottle, liquid evaporates and vapour condenses at equal rates, so the vapour pressure stays steady.

Shape of a Liquid

A liquid gets the shape of its container when it is poured into it, because liquid molecules can slide over each other. A liquid is almost incompressible and has a definite volume, but no definite shape of its own.

mcqs.q: On the basis of kinetic molecular theory, liquid molecules:
options: Are fixed in a regular lattice
Are close together like a solid but can move past one another like a gas
Are far apart with large empty spaces
mcqs.why: Liquids lie between gases and solids: their molecules are close together like a solid, but they can move past one another like a gas, which explains their in-between properties.

mcqs.q: Two liquids mix slowly by diffusion because:
options: Liquid molecules are in constant motion and can move from one place to another
mcqs.why: Diffusion in liquids happens because liquid molecules are in constant motion and can move from one place to another, though more slowly than gas molecules.

mcqs.q: Liquids are almost incompressible because:
options: Their molecules are already close together
mcqs.why: Compression is negligible in liquids because the molecules are already close together, leaving almost no empty space to squeeze out.

mcqs.q: On heating, a liquid expands a little because:
options: Molecular motion increases and the molecules move slightly apart
mcqs.why: On heating, molecular motion increases and the molecules move slightly apart, so liquids expand a little, much less than gases.

mcqs.q: The motion of molecules in a liquid is best described as:
options: Sliding over one another, but not moving freely like gas molecules
mcqs.why: Liquid molecules slide over one another but cannot move freely like gas molecules, because intermolecular forces hold them close together.

mcqs.q: The intermolecular forces in a liquid are:
options: Strong enough to fix the molecules in place
Strong enough to hold the molecules together but weak enough to let them flow
mcqs.why: Forces between liquid molecules are strong enough to hold them together as a liquid but weak enough to let them flow past one another.

mcqs.q: Dynamic equilibrium between two physical states means:
options: One change is faster than the other
The two opposite changes go on at the same time and at equal rates, so the amounts of the two states stay constant
mcqs.why: In dynamic equilibrium the two opposite changes continue at equal rates, so amounts stay constant although molecules keep changing state; it is dynamic, not static.

mcqs.q: In a closed bottle partly filled with liquid, the vapour pressure stays steady because:
options: Liquid evaporates and vapour condenses at equal rates
The bottle is sealed against molecules moving
mcqs.why: In a closed bottle, liquid evaporates and vapour condenses at equal rates, a dynamic equilibrium, so the vapour pressure stays steady.

mcqs.q: A liquid takes the shape of its container because:
options: Its molecules are fixed in place
Its molecules can slide over each other
mcqs.why: A liquid gets the shape of its container when poured into it, because liquid molecules can slide over each other; it has a definite volume but no definite shape of its own.

mcqs.q: A liquid has:
options: A definite volume but no definite shape of its own
A definite shape and a definite volume
No definite volume but a definite shape
mcqs.why: A liquid is almost incompressible and has a definite volume, but no definite shape of its own, taking the shape of its container instead.

lessons.title: Inter-Molecular Forces in Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
The forces between molecules — intermolecular forces — decide whether a substance is a gas, a liquid or a solid at ordinary temperature, and how fast it evaporates. They are weaker than the bonds inside a molecule.

London Dispersion Forces

London forces arise from temporary, instantaneous dipoles. At any instant the electrons in an atom may be unevenly distributed, creating a tiny temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, and the two attract. These forces exist between all molecules, grow stronger with more electrons and larger atoms, and are the only forces between non-polar molecules. London dispersion forces are the only forces present among molecules of solid iodine at room temperature, and among F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2, fluorine (F2) has the weakest London dispersion forces.

Dipole-Dipole Interactions

Dipole-dipole interactions are the attractions between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another polar molecule. They are stronger than London forces but weaker than hydrogen bonds, and they raise the boiling points of polar liquids such as HCl and acetone above those of comparable non-polar liquids.

Hydrogen Bonding

Hydrogen bonding is the strong attraction between a hydrogen atom attached to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. Hydrogen bonding is involved in the structure of DNA, in the liquid properties of water and in liquid HF, but not in liquid CH4. HF is a liquid at ordinary temperature while HCl is a gas, because HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with one another, while HCl molecules have only weak dipole-dipole forces. The exceptionally low acidic strength of HF is due to strong hydrogen bonding.

Neon and Argon

Neon and argon are both mono-atomic noble gases of the same group, but argon atoms are larger and have more electrons than neon atoms, so the London dispersion forces between argon atoms are stronger. More energy is therefore needed to separate argon atoms, giving argon a higher boiling point (-189 degrees C) than neon (-248 degrees C).

Classifying Substances by Intermolecular Force

Sort substances by their strongest intermolecular force: hydrogen bonding for water, milk, honey, methylated spirit, glycerine and ammonia; dipole-dipole for acetone, chloroform and hydrogen chloride; London dispersion only for carbon tetrachloride, benzene, kerosene oil and methane. The force type follows from polarity and the presence of hydrogen attached to N, O or F: the O-H groups in water and glycerine give hydrogen bonding, while the symmetrical CCl4 and C6H6 molecules are non-polar.

mcqs.q: London dispersion forces arise from:
options: Temporary, instantaneous dipoles formed when electrons are unevenly distributed in an atom
mcqs.why: At any instant the electrons in an atom may be unevenly distributed, creating a tiny temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, and the two attract; these are London dispersion forces.

mcqs.q: London dispersion forces:
options: Exist between all molecules, grow stronger with more electrons and larger atoms, and are the only forces between non-polar molecules
mcqs.why: London forces exist between all molecules and are the only forces between non-polar molecules; they grow stronger with more electrons and larger atoms.

mcqs.q: The only intermolecular forces present among molecules of solid iodine are:
mcqs.why: Iodine molecules are non-polar, so London dispersion forces are the only forces present among molecules of solid iodine at room temperature.

mcqs.q: Among F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2, the weakest London dispersion forces are found in:
mcqs.why: London forces grow stronger with more electrons and larger atoms; fluorine (F2) has the smallest atoms and fewest electrons of the four, so it has the weakest London dispersion forces.

mcqs.q: Dipole-dipole interactions are:
options: Attractions between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another, stronger than London forces but weaker than hydrogen bonds
mcqs.why: Dipole-dipole interactions are the attractions between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another; they are stronger than London forces but weaker than hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen bonding is the strong attraction between:
options: A hydrogen atom attached to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen attached to a small, very electronegative atom (N, O or F) attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule, as in water, HF and DNA.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen bonding is NOT involved in:
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding is involved in the structure of DNA, in the liquid properties of water and in liquid HF, but not in liquid CH4, whose molecules are non-polar and held only by London forces.

mcqs.q: HF is a liquid at ordinary temperature while HCl is a gas because:
options: HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with one another, while HCl molecules have only weak dipole-dipole forces
mcqs.why: The strong hydrogen bonds between HF molecules hold them together as a liquid, while HCl molecules have only weak dipole-dipole forces and escape as a gas; the exceptionally low acidic strength of HF is also due to strong hydrogen bonding.

mcqs.q: Argon has a higher boiling point (-189 degrees C) than neon (-248 degrees C) because:
options: Argon atoms are larger and have more electrons, so the London dispersion forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them
mcqs.why: Neon and argon are both mono-atomic noble gases, but argon atoms are larger with more electrons, so their London dispersion forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the atoms.

mcqs.q: The strongest intermolecular force in carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is:
mcqs.why: CCl4 is a symmetrical non-polar molecule, so it is classed with benzene, kerosene oil and methane as having London dispersion only; hydrogen bonding is found in water, glycerine and ammonia, and dipole-dipole forces in acetone, chloroform and HCl.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
Evaporation, vapour pressure, boiling point, viscosity and surface tension are the physical properties that describe a liquid. All of them follow from the strength of the intermolecular forces.

Evaporation

Evaporation is a surface phenomenon and a continuous process. It is not exothermic: evaporation causes cooling, because it takes the fastest molecules from the surface of a liquid, and those molecules carry away kinetic energy, so the average kinetic energy of the molecules left behind falls. Different liquids have different rates of evaporation even at the same temperature, because a liquid with weak forces, like ether, lets its surface molecules escape easily, while a liquid with strong hydrogen bonding, like water, holds its molecules back. Wet clothes dry more quickly on a hot, dry day than on a hot, humid day, because on a humid day the air is already nearly saturated with water vapour, so evaporation is slow.

Vapour Pressure

The vapour pressure of a liquid depends on the intermolecular forces: only molecules with enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractions of their neighbours can escape into the vapour. In a liquid with weak forces many molecules escape, giving a high vapour pressure; in a liquid with strong hydrogen bonding few escape, giving a low vapour pressure. The vapour pressure of a given liquid decreases if the temperature is decreased. Among benzene (80 degrees C), methanol (65 degrees C), aniline (184 degrees C) and nitrobenzene (112 degrees C), methanol shows the highest vapour pressure at room temperature, because it has the lowest boiling point.

Boiling Point

Boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the external pressure. Because of this, the boiling point depends on the external pressure: at higher pressure, as in a pressure cooker, the boiling point rises; at lower pressure, as on a mountain, the boiling point falls, so water boils below 100 degrees C on a mountain. The normal boiling point is measured at 1 atm pressure. During boiling the temperature remains constant although heat is being supplied continuously, because the heat is used to overcome the intermolecular forces and change the liquid into vapour, as latent heat of vaporisation. Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point by lowering the pressure, so a heat-sensitive liquid can be distilled below the temperature at which it would decompose at normal pressure.

Viscosity and Surface Tension

The S.I. unit of viscosity is kg m^-1 s^-1. Surface tension is the result of the intermolecular forces pulling surface molecules inwards, since they have no neighbours above them. The stronger the intermolecular forces, the greater the inward pull and the higher the surface tension. Water, with strong hydrogen bonding, has a high surface tension, while ether, with weak forces, has a low one. A water droplet is spherical because surface tension pulls the surface into the smallest possible area for its volume, and the sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume.

Physical Properties of Water

Water evaporates readily at all temperatures and its vapour pressure rises with temperature; it boils at 100 degrees C at 1 atm because of strong hydrogen bonding. Its viscosity is low but higher than that of non-polar liquids, and its surface tension is high (72.8 mN/m) because surface molecules are pulled inwards by hydrogen bonds.

Why Water Has a High Boiling Point

Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, two through its hydrogen atoms and two through the lone pairs on oxygen, building a wide network. Each HF molecule can form only about two hydrogen bonds on average, so the network in water is stronger and more energy is needed to break it, giving water the higher boiling point despite fluorine being more electronegative. Water and ethanol mix easily in all proportions because both form hydrogen bonds, and the -OH group of ethanol fits into the hydrogen-bonded network of water.

Anomalous Behaviour of Water

Water is unusual because its density increases as it cools down to 4 degrees C and then decreases as it cools further to 0 degrees C, so water has maximum density at 4 degrees C. Below 4 degrees C the molecules begin to form the open hydrogen-bonded structure of ice, which takes up more space, so ice is less dense than water and floats. When water freezes at 0 degrees C its density decreases because of the empty space present in the structure of ice.

Earthenware Vessels

An earthenware vessel is porous, so a little water seeps through its walls and evaporates from the outer surface. Evaporation needs latent heat, which it takes from the water inside, cooling it. The vessel therefore keeps water cool even on hot summer days. If water had weak hydrogen bonding, it would boil at a much lower temperature and evaporate very quickly, and ice would no longer float, disturbing aquatic life.

Volatility Ranking

At the same temperature, volatility falls as intermolecular forces strengthen: London-only liquids escape easily, dipole liquids less easily, and hydrogen-bonded liquids least easily. So methane and kerosene fractions are most volatile, then acetone, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride, then methylated spirit and ammonia, and last water, milk, honey and glycerine, which are least volatile because of their extensive hydrogen bonding and high viscosity.

options: A bulk phenomenon occurring throughout the liquid
A surface phenomenon and a continuous process
Possible only at the boiling point
mcqs.why: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon and a continuous process: it happens at the surface of a liquid at all temperatures, unlike boiling which occurs throughout the liquid.

options: It releases heat to the liquid
It slows all the molecules down chemically
It takes the fastest molecules from the surface, and those molecules carry away kinetic energy, so the average kinetic energy of the molecules left behind falls
mcqs.why: Evaporation is not exothermic: only the fastest surface molecules escape, carrying away kinetic energy, so the average kinetic energy, and hence the temperature, of the liquid left behind falls.

options: The intermolecular forces: weak forces let many molecules escape, giving a high vapour pressure
The size of the container only
mcqs.why: Only molecules with enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractions of their neighbours can escape; in a liquid with weak forces many escape, giving a high vapour pressure, while strong hydrogen bonding gives a low vapour pressure.

mcqs.q: If the temperature of a liquid is decreased, its vapour pressure:
mcqs.why: The vapour pressure of a given liquid decreases if the temperature is decreased, because fewer molecules then have enough kinetic energy to escape from the surface.

mcqs.why: Methanol shows the highest vapour pressure at room temperature because it has the lowest boiling point of the four, meaning its molecules escape most easily.

mcqs.q: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which:
options: The vapour pressure of the liquid becomes equal to the external pressure
mcqs.why: Boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the external pressure; the normal boiling point is measured at 1 atm pressure.

mcqs.q: On a mountain, water boils below 100 degrees C because:
options: There is less water vapour in the air
The external pressure is lower, so the vapour pressure equals it at a lower temperature
mcqs.why: Boiling point depends on external pressure: at lower pressure, as on a mountain, the boiling point falls, while at higher pressure, as in a pressure cooker, the boiling point rises.

mcqs.q: During boiling, the temperature remains constant although heat is supplied continuously because:
options: The heat is lost to the air
The heat is used to overcome the intermolecular forces and change the liquid into vapour, as latent heat of vaporisation
mcqs.why: The supplied heat is used to overcome the intermolecular forces and change the liquid into vapour as latent heat of vaporisation, rather than raising the temperature.

mcqs.q: Vacuum distillation is used for a heat-sensitive liquid because lowering the pressure:
options: Lowers the boiling point, so the liquid can be distilled below the temperature at which it would decompose
mcqs.why: Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point by lowering the pressure, so a heat-sensitive liquid can be distilled below the temperature at which it would decompose at normal pressure.

mcqs.why: The S.I. unit of viscosity is kg m^-1 s^-1; viscosity and surface tension are the remaining physical properties of liquids described in this lesson.

lessons.title: Energetics of Phase Change
lessons.notes_html:
A phase change is a change of a substance from one physical state to another, such as melting, boiling or freezing. Every phase change absorbs or releases a fixed amount of heat at a constant temperature.

Molar Heats of Phase Change

Molar heat of vaporisation is the heat absorbed when one mole of a liquid changes into vapour at its boiling point, in kJ/mol; for water it is 40.7 kJ/mol. Molar heat of fusion is the heat absorbed when one mole of a solid melts at its melting point, in kJ/mol. Molar heat of sublimation is the heat absorbed when one mole of a solid changes directly into vapour, in kJ/mol, and it equals the sum of the heats of fusion and vaporisation. The heat is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to raise the temperature.

All Possible Phase Changes

The possible changes among vapour, liquid and solid are: solid to liquid (melting), liquid to solid (freezing), liquid to vapour (vaporisation), vapour to liquid (condensation), solid to vapour (sublimation) and vapour to solid (deposition or reverse sublimation).

mcqs.q: A phase change is:
options: A change of a substance from one physical state to another, absorbing or releasing a fixed amount of heat at a constant temperature
A change in the composition of a substance
mcqs.why: Every phase change, such as melting, boiling or freezing, absorbs or releases a fixed amount of heat at a constant temperature while the state changes.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of vaporisation is:
options: The heat released when one mole of vapour condenses
The heat needed to raise one mole by 1 degree
Measured in kJ only for solids
The heat absorbed when one mole of a liquid changes into vapour at its boiling point, 40.7 kJ/mol for water
mcqs.why: Molar heat of vaporisation is the heat absorbed when one mole of a liquid changes into vapour at its boiling point, in kJ/mol; for water it is 40.7 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of fusion is:
options: The heat absorbed when one mole of a solid melts at its melting point
The heat released when one mole freezes at any temperature
The heat of combustion of one mole
mcqs.why: Molar heat of fusion is the heat absorbed when one mole of a solid melts at its melting point, in kJ/mol; the heat is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to raise the temperature.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of sublimation is equal to:
options: Heat of fusion minus heat of vaporisation
The sum of the heats of fusion and vaporisation
mcqs.why: Sublimation takes a solid directly to vapour, passing in effect through melting and then vaporisation, so the molar heat of sublimation equals the sum of the heats of fusion and vaporisation.

mcqs.q: During a phase change, the heat absorbed is used to:
options: Overcome intermolecular forces, not to raise the temperature
Break covalent bonds in every case
mcqs.why: The heat of a phase change is used to overcome intermolecular forces while the temperature stays constant, which is why melting and boiling occur at fixed temperatures.

mcqs.q: The direct change of a solid into vapour is called:
mcqs.why: Solid to vapour is sublimation, and the reverse change, vapour to solid, is deposition or reverse sublimation; the other changes are melting, freezing, vaporisation and condensation.

mcqs.q: The change of vapour directly into solid is called:
mcqs.why: Vapour to solid is deposition or reverse sublimation, one of the six possible changes among vapour, liquid and solid listed in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the change from liquid to solid?
mcqs.why: Liquid to solid is freezing, the reverse of melting (solid to liquid); liquid to vapour is vaporisation and vapour to liquid is condensation.

mcqs.q: The molar heats of phase change are expressed in:
mcqs.why: Molar heats of vaporisation, fusion and sublimation are all quoted per mole, in kJ/mol, for example 40.7 kJ/mol for the vaporisation of water.

mcqs.q: When one mole of a liquid boils at its boiling point, the temperature during the change:
options: Remains constant while the heat is absorbed
mcqs.why: A phase change absorbs or releases a fixed amount of heat at a constant temperature; the heat overcomes intermolecular forces instead of raising the temperature.

lessons.title: Liquid Crystals
lessons.notes_html:
Liquid crystals are a state of matter between liquid and solid. They flow like liquids but keep some of the order of a crystal.

Definition

Liquid crystals are substances that flow like liquids but keep some order of a crystal. Their molecules are arranged in a regular pattern in one direction while moving freely in other directions, so they behave partly like a liquid and partly like a solid crystal.

Comparison with Pure Liquids and Crystalline Solids

Pure liquids have no regular arrangement of molecules and flow freely in all directions. Crystalline solids have a fully regular three-dimensional arrangement and a fixed shape. Liquid crystals lie between the two: they flow like liquids but their molecules keep a partial order, like crystals, in at least one direction. Among ionic, solid, liquid and molecular crystals, liquid crystals are the most temperature sensitive.

Uses in Daily Life

Liquid crystals are used in the displays of watches, calculators, mobile phones, televisions and laptops, where an electric field changes their alignment to form letters and pictures. They are also used in thermometers that change colour with temperature, in medical imaging, and in optical shutters.

mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are a state of matter between liquid and solid: they flow like liquids but keep some order of a crystal.

options: Fixed in a full three-dimensional lattice
Arranged in a regular pattern in one direction while moving freely in other directions
mcqs.why: The molecules of a liquid crystal are arranged in a regular pattern in one direction while moving freely in other directions, so they behave partly like a liquid and partly like a solid crystal.

options: Have no regular arrangement of molecules and flow freely in all directions
mcqs.why: Pure liquids have no regular arrangement of molecules and flow freely in all directions, while crystalline solids have a fully regular three-dimensional arrangement and a fixed shape; liquid crystals lie between the two.

A fully regular three-dimensional arrangement and a fixed shape

mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are the most temperature sensitive among ionic, solid, liquid and molecular crystals, which is why they are used in thermometers that change colour with temperature.

An electric field changes the alignment of the liquid crystal molecules
mcqs.why: An electric field changes the alignment of the molecules in the display, and the changed alignment forms the letters and pictures seen on the screen.

options: Thermometers that change colour with temperature, medical imaging and optical shutters
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are also used in thermometers that change colour with temperature, in medical imaging, and in optical shutters, besides their display applications.

options: Flow like liquids but their molecules keep a partial order, like crystals, in at least one direction
mcqs.why: This in-between behaviour, flowing like a liquid while keeping partial crystalline order in at least one direction, is the defining feature of liquid crystals.

options: In at least one direction, while the molecules move freely in other directions
mcqs.why: Their molecules are arranged in a regular pattern in one direction while moving freely in other directions, so the order is partial, unlike the full three-dimensional order of a crystal.

lessons.title: Kinetic Molecular Interpretation of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
In a solid the particles are closely packed and cannot move freely; they only vibrate about their mean positions, so kinetic energy exists as vibrational energy. The close packing gives solids a definite shape and volume, minimum empty space, negligible diffusion and almost no compressibility.

Properties from Kinetic Molecular Theory

(i) Diffusion is negligible because particles cannot leave their positions. (ii) Compression is negligible because particles are already in contact. (iii) Expansion is small because heating only increases the amplitude of vibration. (iv) Motion of molecules is vibration about fixed mean positions, not free movement.

mcqs.q: In a solid, the particles:
options: Move freely through the whole volume
Are closely packed and only vibrate about their mean positions
Slide over one another like a liquid
mcqs.why: In a solid the particles are closely packed and cannot move freely; they only vibrate about their mean positions, so kinetic energy exists as vibrational energy.

mcqs.q: The kinetic energy of particles in a solid exists as:
mcqs.why: Because solid particles cannot leave their positions, their kinetic energy exists as vibrational energy, vibration about fixed mean positions.

mcqs.q: Diffusion in solids is negligible because:
mcqs.why: Diffusion is negligible in solids because the particles are locked in the lattice and cannot leave their positions to mix with other particles.

mcqs.q: Compression of a solid is negligible because:
options: Solids are very hard only at low temperature
The particles are already in contact, with minimum empty space
mcqs.why: Compression is negligible because particles are already in contact in a closely packed solid; the close packing gives minimum empty space.

mcqs.q: On heating, a solid expands only slightly because heating:
options: Only increases the amplitude of vibration of the particles
mcqs.why: Expansion is small in solids because heating only increases the amplitude of vibration about the fixed mean positions; the particles stay in place.

mcqs.q: The close packing of particles gives solids:
mcqs.why: The close packing gives solids a definite shape and volume, minimum empty space, negligible diffusion and almost no compressibility.

mcqs.q: The motion of molecules in a solid is:
options: Free movement from place to place
Vibration about fixed mean positions, not free movement
mcqs.why: Motion of molecules in a solid is vibration about fixed mean positions, not free movement; this is the kinetic molecular interpretation of solids in this lesson.

mcqs.q: A solid does not flow like a liquid because its particles:
options: Cannot move freely or leave their positions
mcqs.why: Flow needs particles to move past one another; solid particles only vibrate about their mean positions and cannot leave them, so solids keep a definite shape.

mcqs.q: When a solid is heated, the amplitude of vibration of its particles:
options: Turns into free motion at once
mcqs.why: Heating increases the amplitude of vibration, pushing neighbouring particles slightly farther apart on average, which is why expansion of a solid is small.

mcqs.q: Compared with gases and liquids, the empty space between particles in a solid is:
options: Minimum, because the particles are closely packed
mcqs.why: The close packing in solids gives minimum empty space, which is why solids are almost incompressible and have negligible diffusion.

lessons.title: Types of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Solids are of two kinds: crystalline solids, with a regular arrangement of particles, and amorphous solids, with no regular arrangement.

Crystalline and Amorphous Solids

Crystalline solids have a regular arrangement of particles, a definite geometrical shape, sharp melting points, cleavage planes and anisotropy. Amorphous solids have no regular arrangement, no definite shape, soften over a range of temperature instead of melting sharply, and show no cleavage planes or anisotropy, like glass and plastic. Household items can be classified by these tests: table salt, sugar, washing soda, baking soda and ice are crystalline, with regular shapes and sharp melting points, while glass is amorphous, with no regular shape, no sharp melting point and no cleavage planes.

Why Crystalline Solids Have a Sharp Melting Point

All the particles in a crystalline solid are held by identical forces in a regular lattice, so at one fixed temperature all the bonds break together and the whole solid melts at once. The melting point is therefore sharp. In an amorphous solid the forces differ from place to place, so it softens gradually over a range of temperature.

Ionic, Covalent, Molecular and Metallic Solids

Ionic solids are built from ions held by strong electrostatic forces, so they are hard with high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved. Covalent solids have atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout, so they are very hard with very high melting points, like diamond. Molecular solids have molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, so they are soft with low melting points, like ice, iodine and sugar. lessons.title: Properties of Crystalline Solids
lessons.notes_html:
A crystal has a definite shape because its particles repeat in a regular pattern. That regularity gives crystals five characteristic properties.

Habit, Cleavage, Growth, Anisotropy, Symmetry

Habit of a crystal is the shape in which it usually grows, such as the cubes of NaCl. Cleavage planes are the planes along which a crystal splits cleanly when struck, because the bonds are weakest there. Crystal growth proceeds by adding layers of particles to the faces of a seed crystal. Anisotropy means properties vary with direction in the crystal. Symmetry means the crystal looks unchanged after rotation, reflection or inversion through a centre of symmetry; a cubic crystal has one centre of symmetry.

Anisotropy

In a crystalline solid the particles are arranged regularly, so the distances and forces between particles differ in different directions. A property such as electrical conductivity, refractive index or cleavage therefore has different values when measured along different directions of the crystal, which is anisotropy. Crystals show variation in physical properties depending upon the direction; that property is called anisotropy. When a crystalline substance conducts current in one direction but not through other directions of the crystal, this property is anisotropy. The opposite property, the same value in all directions, is isotropy.

Transition Temperature

Transition temperature is the temperature at which one crystalline form of a substance changes into another form, both forms existing together in equilibrium at that temperature. Examples are sulphur, rhombic changing to monoclinic at 95.6 degrees C, and tin, grey changing to white at 13.2 degrees C. Crystals of the same substance can co-exist in equilibrium with each other at its transition temperature.

Isomorphism and Polymorphism

Polymorphism is the occurrence of the same substance in more than one crystalline form, such as rhombic and monoclinic sulphur. Isomorphism is the occurrence of different substances in the same crystalline form, such as NaNO3 and CaCO3. Polymorphism concerns one substance in many forms; isomorphism concerns many substances in one form. Isomorphic substances usually have the same atomic ratio: KNO3 and NaNO3 both have the atomic ratio 1:1:3 and the same crystal form. A pair of compounds which are isomorphic in nature is MgO and ZnO.

Allotropy

Allotropy is the occurrence of an element in more than one form in the same physical state. Oxygen exists as O2 and as ozone O3, which differ in properties although both are oxygen. Sulphur exists as rhombic sulphur and monoclinic sulphur, which have different crystal shapes and change into each other at 95.6 degrees C.

lessons.title: Types of Crystalline Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Crystalline solids fall into four types, decided by the particles in the lattice and the forces holding them together.

Comparison of the Four Types

TypeParticlesForcesProperties
IonicIonsElectrostaticHard, high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved
CovalentAtomsCovalent bondsVery hard, very high melting point, like diamond
MolecularMoleculesWeak van der Waals forcesSoft, low melting point, like ice and sugar
MetallicPositive ions in electron seaMetallic bondConducts heat and electricity, malleable, ductile

Why Covalent Crystals Are Hard and Molecular Crystals Are Soft

In a covalent crystal every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds running through the whole crystal, as in diamond, so the crystal is very hard. In a molecular crystal the molecules are held only by weak van der Waals forces, which break easily, so the crystal is soft and melts at a low temperature. The nature of the bonds between atoms in graphite is covalent.

Why Metallic Crystals Conduct but Ionic Crystals Do Not

In a metallic crystal the valence electrons are free to move through the whole crystal as a sea of electrons, so an electric current flows easily. In an ionic crystal the ions are fixed in their lattice positions in the solid state and cannot move, so solid ionic crystals do not conduct; they conduct only when molten or dissolved, when the ions become free. In the solid state, metallic crystals are the good conductors of heat and electricity.

Sodium Chloride Lattice

Sodium chloride forms a face-centred cubic lattice. Each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl- ions and each Cl- ion by six Na+ ions, so the coordination number is 6:6. The unit cell contains four Na+ and four Cl- ions, that is four formula units of NaCl. The ions are arranged so that the crystal cleaves along planes and grows as cubes.

Lattice Energy

Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its gaseous ions of opposite charge. For example, the lattice energy of NaCl is about 787 kJ/mol and of MgO about 3795 kJ/mol, the higher value for MgO reflecting the doubly charged ions. Lattice energy is an energy, while a crystal lattice is the arrangement of the particles themselves.

Low Density and High Heat of Fusion of Ice

Ice has a low density because its water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds in an open cage-like structure with large empty spaces, so ice occupies more volume than the same mass of water and floats. Ice has a high heat of fusion because melting must break a large number of hydrogen bonds, which needs a great deal of energy, 6.0 kJ per mole.

lessons.title: Crystal Lattice
lessons.notes_html:
A crystal lattice is the regular three-dimensional arrangement of points that represent the positions of particles in a crystal. The unit cell is the smallest portion of that lattice which, repeated in all directions, reproduces the whole crystal.

Unit Cell and Crystal Lattice

A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal; repeating it in three dimensions builds the whole crystal and decides its shape. In NaCl the unit cell is face-centred cubic: the whole crystal grows by repeating this cubic cell, so the NaCl crystal itself is cubic in shape. The parameters of a unit cell are 6: three edge lengths and three angles. The unit cell of NaCl is a cube with Cl- ions at the corners and face centres and Na+ ions at the edge centres and the body centre, giving four formula units per cell.

Packing Arrangements

The three packing arrangements are simple cubic packing, in which each sphere touches six neighbours and much space is wasted; body-centred cubic packing, in which each sphere touches eight neighbours; and face-centred cubic or close packing, in which each sphere touches twelve neighbours and the packing is most efficient. Models are built by stacking equal balls, such as marbles, in each pattern and comparing the empty space left.

Factors Affecting the Shape of an Ionic Crystal

Three factors are the relative sizes (radius ratio) of the cation and anion, which decides the coordination number; the charges on the ions, which decide the strength of the lattice; and the conditions of temperature and pressure during crystallisation, which can favour one form over another.

Plane and Axis of Symmetry

A plane of symmetry divides a crystal into two mirror halves, while an axis of symmetry is a line about which rotation leaves the crystal looking unchanged.

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.notes_html:
Many reactions do not go to completion: the products react back to give the reactants again. When the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, the system is in equilibrium.

Dynamic Equilibrium

In a closed vessel at constant temperature, liquid evaporates and vapour condenses at the same time. When the two rates become equal, the amount of liquid and vapour stays constant, but molecules keep passing both ways across the surface. The equilibrium is therefore dynamic, not static: nothing appears to change, yet both processes continue.

Equilibrium Constant Kc

The equilibrium constant Kc is the ratio of the concentrations of products to reactants, each raised to its coefficient, at equilibrium. For A + B (reversible) C + D, Kc = [C][D] / ([A][B]). The Law of Mass Action states that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants. For A + B (reversible) C + D, forward rate = kf[A][B] and reverse rate = kr[C][D]; at equilibrium the rates are equal, so kf[A][B] = kr[C][D], giving Kc = kf / kr = [C][D] / ([A][B]).

What Kc Tells About Extent

If Kc is very large, such as 10^30, the reaction goes to completion in the forward direction. If Kc is very small, such as 10^-30, the reaction hardly proceeds: chlorine molecules decompose to a very small extent into atomic chlorine, Cl2 (reversible) 2Cl, because Kc of this reaction is very small. If Kc is neither large nor small, an appreciable amount of both products and reactants is present. When Kc = 1 for A + B (reversible) C + D, the reaction is 50 percent complete. For the reaction 2O3 (reversible) 3O2, Kc = 1.0 x 10^50 at 25 degrees C, so the reaction goes virtually to completion: at room temperature ozone is almost completely converted into oxygen.

Predicting Direction with Q

Compare the reaction quotient Q with Kc: if Q is less than Kc the reaction goes forward, if Q is greater than Kc it goes backward, and if Q equals Kc it is at equilibrium.

Kc for Common Reactions

(i) PCl5(g) (reversible) PCl3(g) + Cl2(g): Kc = [PCl3][Cl2] / [PCl5]. (ii) 2HI(g) (reversible) H2(g) + I2(g): Kc = [H2][I2] / [HI]^2. (iii) H2(g) + CO2(g) (reversible) CO(g) + H2O(g): Kc = [CO][H2O] / ([H2][CO2]). (iv) 2N2O5(g) (reversible) 4NO2(g) + O2(g): Kc = [NO2]^4 [O2] / [N2O5]^2. In each case the products are on top and the reactants below, each raised to its coefficient.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: A mixture of 0.5 moles of H2 and I2 each was placed in a one litre flask at 400 degrees C. Calculate the concentration of H2, I2 and HI at equilibrium. The Kc for the reaction is 54.3. Solution: Step 1: H2 + I2 (reversible) 2HI. Let x mol react: [H2] = [I2] = 0.5 - x, [HI] = 2x. Step 2: Kc = [HI]^2 / ([H2][I2]) = (2x)^2 / (0.5 - x)^2 = 54.3. Step 3: Taking square roots, 2x / (0.5 - x) = 7.369, so 2x = 3.6845 - 7.369x, giving x = 0.3933. Step 4: [H2] = [I2] = 0.5 - 0.3933 = 0.107 M, [HI] = 0.786 M. Answers as printed in the book.

Numerical 2: The equilibrium mixture contains 1 mole of PCl5, 0.3 mole of PCl3 and 0.08 mole of Cl2 in a 10 L flask. Calculate Kc. Solution: Step 1: Concentrations: [PCl5] = 1/10 = 0.1 M, [PCl3] = 0.3/10 = 0.03 M, [Cl2] = 0.08/10 = 0.008 M. Step 2: Kc = [PCl3][Cl2] / [PCl5] = (0.03 x 0.008) / 0.1 = 2.40 x 10^-3. Answer: Kc = 2.40 x 10^-3.

Numerical 3: The equilibrium concentration of N2 and O2 is 0.25 M each while its Kc is 0.1 at 2000 degrees C. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of NO for N2(g) + O2(g) (reversible) 2NO(g). Solution: Step 1: Kc = [NO]^2 / ([N2][O2]) = 0.1. Step 2: [NO]^2 = 0.1 x 0.25 x 0.25 = 0.00625. Step 3: [NO] = sqrt(0.00625) = 0.079 M. Answer: [NO] = 0.079 M.

Numerical 4: For the reaction 2SO2(g) + O2(g) (reversible) 2SO3(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [SO2] = 0.90 M, [O2] = 0.35 M and [SO3] = 1.1 M. Calculate Kc. Solution: Step 1: Kc = [SO3]^2 / ([SO2]^2 [O2]) = (1.1)^2 / ((0.90)^2 x 0.35) = 1.21 / 0.2835 = 4.27. Answer: about 4.3, as printed in the book.

Numerical 5: The equilibrium concentrations of N2, O2 and NO are 0.05 M, 0.05 M, and 5.5 x 10^-4 M respectively. Calculate Kc for the decomposition of NO at 1500 degrees C, 2NO (reversible) N2 + O2. Solution: Kc = [N2][O2] / [NO]^2 = (0.05 x 0.05) / (5.5 x 10^-4)^2 = 0.0025 / 3.025 x 10^-7 = 8.26 x 10^3. Note: the book's printed exponent reads 10^9 in the scan, which does not follow from the given concentrations; the worked value is 10^3.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Equilibrium (Le-Chatelier's Principle)
lessons.notes_html:
Le-Chatelier's principle states that if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts to reduce the stress. It applies to physical and chemical systems at equilibrium. Only a change in temperature changes Kc permanently, because Kc is a constant at a given temperature.

Effect of Concentration

Adding a reactant or removing a product disturbs the equilibrium, and the system shifts to restore the ratio of products to reactants given by Kc. Once the new equilibrium is reached, the ratio is the same as before, so Kc itself is unchanged: a change in concentration does not change the value of the equilibrium constant permanently.

Effect of Pressure

Pressure affects only equilibria with different numbers of moles of gas on the two sides. (i) N2(g) + O2(g) (reversible) 2NO(g): no effect, because both sides have 2 moles of gas, so pressure cannot favour either side. The change in temperature changes the equilibrium position of this reaction but a change in pressure does not, for the same reason. (ii) PCl5(g) (reversible) PCl3(g) + Cl2(g): shifts backwards, because the forward side has 2 moles against 1 mole of reactant, so higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles, the reactants. (iii) 2NO2(g) (reversible) N2O4(g): shifts forwards, because 2 moles become 1 mole, so higher pressure favours the product. (iv) 2SO2(g) + O2(g) (reversible) 2SO3(g): shifts forwards, because 3 moles become 2 moles, so higher pressure favours the product.

Effect of Temperature

Raising the temperature shifts an exothermic forward reaction backwards and an endothermic forward reaction forwards. For N2 + 3H2 (reversible) 2NH3, delta H is negative, so heating reduces NH3. For 2NO + O2 (reversible) 2NO2, delta H is negative, so heating reduces NO2. For 2SO2 + O2 (reversible) 2SO3, delta H is negative, so heating reduces SO3. For N2 + O2 (reversible) 2NO, delta H is positive, so heating increases NO. Endothermic reactions are favoured in the forward direction by heating. The value of Kc falls with the rise in temperature for the synthesis of SO3, 2SO2(g) + O2(g) (reversible) 2SO3(g), delta H = -94.58 kJ/mol, because raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, so less SO3 is formed at equilibrium and Kc becomes smaller.

Effect of Catalyst

A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the value of Kc; it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster. For example, adding a catalyst does not increase the yield of SO3 from SO2 and oxygen, while adding more SO2 does.

Kp and Kc

For aA + bB (reversible) cC + dD, Kp = (pC^c pD^d) / (pA^a pB^b) and Kc = ([C]^c [D]^d) / ([A]^a [B]^b). From the ideal gas law, p = [gas] RT, so each partial pressure is replaced by concentration times RT. This gives Kp = Kc (RT)^delta n, where delta n is the change in moles of gas. If delta n = 0, Kp = Kc. The value of Kp is greater than Kc when the difference of the moles of the products and reactants is positive. Units of Kp follow delta n: (a) PCl5 (reversible) PCl3 + Cl2, delta n = +1, so Kp has units of atm. (b) N2 + 3H2 (reversible) 2NH3, delta n = -2, so Kp has units of atm^-2. (c) H2 + CO2 (reversible) CO + H2O, delta n = 0, so Kp has no units. (d) 4NH3 + 5O2 (reversible) 4NO + 6H2O, delta n = +1, so Kp has units of atm. The unit of Kc for PCl5 (reversible) PCl3 + Cl2 is mol/dm^3.

Worked Numerical

Numerical: Calculate Kc for the synthesis of ammonia at 500 degrees C, given Kp = 1.44 x 10^-5. Solution: Step 1: For N2 + 3H2 (reversible) 2NH3, delta n = 2 - 4 = -2. Step 2: Kc = Kp (RT)^-delta n = Kp (RT)^2. Step 3: T = 500 + 273 = 773 K, RT = 0.0821 x 773 = 63.46. Step 4: Kc = 1.44 x 10^-5 x (63.46)^2 = 1.44 x 10^-5 x 4027 = 5.8 x 10^-2. Answer: 5.8 x 10^-2.

Chromate and Dichromate Project

Add about 10 cm^3 of potassium chromate (K2CrO4) solution to two test tubes and note the yellow colour. Add dilute HCl to the second test tube until the colour changes from yellow to orange, then add a few cm^3 of dilute NaOH and the yellow colour appears again. The reaction is 2CrO4^2-(aq) + 2H+(aq) (reversible) Cr2O7^2-(aq) + H2O (yellow to orange). Adding acid increases H+ ions, so by Le-Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the right, and the yellow chromate turns into orange dichromate. Adding base removes H+ ions (forming water), so the equilibrium shifts back to the left, and the yellow chromate colour returns. Le-Chatelier's principle governs both shifts.

mcqs.q: Le-Chatelier's principle states that if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium:
options: The equilibrium shifts to reduce the stress
mcqs.why: Le-Chatelier's principle states that if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts to reduce the stress; it applies to physical and chemical systems at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: The only change that changes Kc permanently is a change in:
mcqs.why: Kc is a constant at a given temperature; only a change in temperature changes Kc permanently, because concentration, pressure and catalyst changes only shift the position.

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure on N2(g) + O2(g) (reversible) 2NO(g) at equilibrium:
options: Has no effect, because both sides have 2 moles of gas
mcqs.why: Pressure affects only equilibria with different numbers of moles of gas on the two sides; here both sides have 2 moles, so pressure cannot favour either side, though a temperature change does shift this reaction.

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure on PCl5(g) (reversible) PCl3(g) + Cl2(g) shifts the equilibrium:
options: Backward, because higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles, the reactants

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure on 2NO2(g) (reversible) N2O4(g) shifts the equilibrium:
mcqs.why: In 2NO2 (reversible) N2O4, 2 moles become 1 mole, so higher pressure favours the product and the equilibrium shifts forwards; the same applies to 2SO2 + O2 (reversible) 2SO3.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 (reversible) 2NH3, delta H is negative. Heating the equilibrium mixture:
options: Reduces NH3, because heating shifts an exothermic forward reaction backwards
mcqs.why: Raising the temperature shifts an exothermic forward reaction backwards and an endothermic forward reaction forwards; since ammonia synthesis is exothermic, heating reduces NH3.

mcqs.q: For N2 + O2 (reversible) 2NO, delta H is positive. Heating:
options: Increases NO, because the forward reaction is endothermic
mcqs.why: Endothermic reactions are favoured in the forward direction by heating; delta H is positive for NO formation, so heating increases NO, unlike the exothermic syntheses of NH3, NO2 and SO3.

mcqs.q: A catalyst added to a system at equilibrium:
options: Does not change the position of equilibrium or the value of Kc; it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster
mcqs.why: A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the value of Kc; for example, adding a catalyst does not increase the yield of SO3 from SO2 and oxygen, while adding more SO2 does.

mcqs.why: For N2 + 3H2 (reversible) 2NH3, delta n = 2 - 4 = -2, so Kc = Kp (RT)^2. With T = 773 K, RT = 0.0821 x 773 = 63.46, and 63.46^2 = 4027. Then Kc = Kp x (RT)^2, that is 1.44 x 10^-5 multiplied by 4027, giving 5.8 x 10^-2.

lessons.title: Industrial Application of Le-Chatelier's Principle (Haber's Process)
lessons.notes_html:
Le-Chatelier's principle is used in industry to choose the temperature, pressure and catalyst that give the best yield of a product. The Haber process for ammonia is the classic example.

Haber's Process

The reaction is N2(g) + 3H2(g) (reversible) 2NH3(g), delta H = -92.46 kJ/mol. It is exothermic, and 4 moles of gas become 2 moles. Low temperature and high pressure therefore favour ammonia, and an iron catalyst is used to reach equilibrium faster. In practice a compromise is used: the optimum temperature for the production of ammonia is 450 degrees C, with a pressure of about 200 atm. A lower temperature would give a better yield but the reaction would be too slow, so 450 degrees C is chosen.

Contact Process for SO3

In the production of SO3 from SO2 and oxygen, the yield of SO3 is increased by adding more SO2. The synthesis 2SO2 + O2 (reversible) 2SO3 is exothermic (delta H = -94.58 kJ/mol), so raising the temperature lowers Kc and reduces the yield; industry therefore uses a moderate temperature with a catalyst.

options: Exothermic, with 4 moles of gas becoming 2 moles
mcqs.why: Ammonia synthesis is exothermic (delta H negative) and 4 moles of gas become 2 moles, so low temperature and high pressure favour ammonia by Le-Chatelier's principle.

mcqs.q: In the Haber process, high pressure favours ammonia because:
options: 4 moles of gas become 2 moles, so higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles
mcqs.why: Pressure affects equilibria with different mole numbers on the two sides; since 4 moles of reactants give 2 moles of NH3, high pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.

mcqs.q: The optimum temperature used in the Haber process is:
mcqs.why: In practice a compromise is used: the optimum temperature for the production of ammonia is 450 degrees C, with a pressure of about 200 atm.

mcqs.q: A lower temperature than 450 degrees C is not used in the Haber process because:
options: It would give a worse yield
It would give a better yield but the reaction would be too slow
mcqs.why: Low temperature favours the exothermic synthesis, but at too low a temperature the reaction is too slow to be economical, so 450 degrees C is chosen as a compromise.

mcqs.q: The pressure used in the Haber process is about:
mcqs.why: The Haber process runs at a pressure of about 200 atm together with the compromise temperature of 450 degrees C and an iron catalyst.

mcqs.q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is:
mcqs.why: An iron catalyst is used to reach equilibrium faster; it does not change the yield given by the equilibrium, only the speed of reaching it.

mcqs.q: The role of the catalyst in the Haber process is to:
options: Increase the equilibrium yield of ammonia
Lower the pressure needed by changing delta n
Help the system reach equilibrium faster, without changing the position of equilibrium
mcqs.why: A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or Kc; in the Haber process the iron catalyst only makes the equilibrium mixture form faster at the compromise conditions.

mcqs.q: In the Contact process, the yield of SO3 from SO2 and oxygen is increased by:
mcqs.why: By Le-Chatelier's principle, adding more SO2 shifts 2SO2 + O2 (reversible) 2SO3 towards the product, increasing the yield of SO3; adding a catalyst alone would not.

mcqs.q: The synthesis 2SO2 + O2 (reversible) 2SO3 has delta H = -94.58 kJ/mol. Raising the temperature:
options: Lowers Kc and reduces the yield, because the endothermic reverse reaction is favoured
Increases the yield but lowers Kc
mcqs.why: The value of Kc falls with rise in temperature for the synthesis of SO3, because raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, so less SO3 is formed at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: For the industrial production of SO3, the conditions chosen are:
options: A moderate temperature with a catalyst
The highest possible temperature without a catalyst
mcqs.why: Industry uses a moderate temperature with a catalyst for SO3 production, balancing the better yield at low temperature against the faster rate at higher temperature, as in the Haber process.

lessons.title: Solubility Product
lessons.notes_html:
A sparingly soluble salt in contact with water sets up an equilibrium between the solid and its ions in solution. Only a very small amount dissolves, and the solution soon becomes saturated, so the rate of dissolving equals the rate of crystallisation. The equilibrium is described by the solubility product, Ksp.

Definition

The solubility product (Ksp) of a sparingly soluble salt is the product of the molar concentrations of its ions in a saturated solution, each raised to the power of its coefficient. For example, for AgCl(s) (reversible) Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq), Ksp = [Ag+][Cl-] = 1.8 x 10^-10 at 25 degrees C. If the ionic product exceeds Ksp, the salt precipitates; if it is less, more salt dissolves.

Ksp Expressions

AgBr (reversible) Ag+ + Br-: Ksp = [Ag+][Br-]. CaCO3 (reversible) Ca2+ + CO3^2-: Ksp = [Ca2+][CO3^2-]. Al(OH)3 (reversible) Al3+ + 3OH-: Ksp = [Al3+][OH-]^3. PbCrO4 (reversible) Pb2+ + CrO4^2-: Ksp = [Pb2+][CrO4^2-].

Solubility from Ksp

For a sparingly soluble salt AB, the solubility product is Ksp = [A+][B-] = s x s = s^2, where s is the solubility in mol/dm^3, so s = sqrt(Ksp). For AgCl with Ksp = 1.8 x 10^-10, s = sqrt(1.8 x 10^-10) = 1.34 x 10^-5 mol/dm^3. For a salt like PbCl2, Ksp = 4s^3, so s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3).

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: The solubility of CaF2 in water at 25 degrees C is found to be 2.05 x 10^-4 M. What is the Ksp at this temperature? Solution: Step 1: CaF2 (reversible) Ca2+ + 2F-, so if solubility is s, [Ca2+] = s and [F-] = 2s. Step 2: Ksp = [Ca2+][F-]^2 = s x (2s)^2 = 4s^3. Step 3: Ksp = 4 x (2.05 x 10^-4)^3 = 3.446 x 10^-11. Answer: 3.446 x 10^-11, as printed in the book.

Numerical 2: The solubility product of AgCl is 1.8 x 10^-10. Calculate the molar solubility of the salt. Solution: Step 1: AgCl (reversible) Ag+ + Cl-, so Ksp = s x s = s^2, where s is the molar solubility. Step 2: s = sqrt(Ksp) = sqrt(1.8 x 10^-10) = 1.34 x 10^-5 M. Answer: 1.34 x 10^-5 M, as printed in the book.

The product of the molar concentrations of its ions in a saturated solution, each raised to the power of its coefficient

mcqs.why: PbCrO4 dissociates into one Pb2+ and one CrO4^2-, so Ksp = [Pb2+][CrO4^2-], like AgBr and CaCO3 which also give two ions with coefficient 1.

mcqs.why: s = sqrt(Ksp) = sqrt(1.8 x 10^-10) = 1.34 x 10^-5 M, as printed in the book.

mcqs.q: For a salt like PbCl2, Ksp is related to solubility s by:
mcqs.why: PbCl2 gives one Pb2+ (s) and two Cl- (2s), so Ksp = s x (2s)^2 = 4 s^3, and s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3).

mcqs.q: The solubility of CaF2 at 25 degrees C is 2.05 x 10^-4 M. Its Ksp is:
A solution is saturated with a sparingly soluble salt when:
options: The rate of dissolving equals the rate of crystallisation
No more salt is present as solid
mcqs.why: Only a very small amount dissolves and the solution soon becomes saturated, so the rate of dissolving equals the rate of crystallisation, and the equilibrium is described by Ksp.

lessons.title: Common Ion Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte when a strong electrolyte containing a common ion is added to its solution.

Examples

Adding NH4Cl to NH4OH solution increases NH4+ ions, so the equilibrium NH4OH (reversible) NH4+ + OH- shifts backwards and the ionisation of NH4OH is suppressed. Adding HCl to H2S solution suppresses the ionisation of H2S, because H+ is the common ion. The ionisation of calcium oxalate is suppressed by adding CaCl2 to it: calcium oxalate ionises as CaC2O4 (reversible) Ca2+ + C2O4^2-, and adding CaCl2 adds Ca2+ ions, which are common to the salt, so by Le-Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts backwards to keep Ksp constant, and the solubility falls.

Use in Purification

Common ion effect is used to purify substances by precipitation. For example, pure NaCl is obtained by passing HCl gas through a saturated solution of impure NaCl: the Cl- ion is common to both, so the equilibrium NaCl(s) (reversible) Na+ + Cl- shifts backwards and pure NaCl precipitates, leaving soluble impurities in solution.

mcqs.q: The common ion effect is:
options: The increase of ionisation by adding a common ion
The suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte when a strong electrolyte containing a common ion is added
The effect of temperature on ions
mcqs.why: The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte when a strong electrolyte containing a common ion is added to its solution.

mcqs.q: Adding NH4Cl to NH4OH solution suppresses the ionisation of NH4OH because:
options: NH4Cl increases NH4+ ions, so the equilibrium NH4OH (reversible) NH4+ + OH- shifts backwards
mcqs.why: The added NH4+ is common to the ionisation equilibrium of NH4OH, so by Le-Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts backwards and the ionisation of NH4OH is suppressed.

mcqs.q: Adding HCl to an H2S solution suppresses the ionisation of H2S because:
mcqs.why: The ionisation of H2S produces H+ ions, and HCl adds more H+, the common ion, so the equilibrium shifts backwards and the ionisation of H2S is suppressed.

mcqs.q: Adding CaCl2 to a solution of calcium oxalate:
options: Suppresses its ionisation and lowers its solubility, because Ca2+ is a common ion and the equilibrium shifts backwards to keep Ksp constant
mcqs.why: Calcium oxalate ionises as CaC2O4 (reversible) Ca2+ + C2O4^2-; adding CaCl2 adds common Ca2+ ions, so the equilibrium shifts backwards and the solubility falls while Ksp stays constant.

mcqs.q: Pure NaCl is obtained from impure saturated NaCl solution by:
options: Passing HCl gas through it, so pure NaCl precipitates by the common ion effect
mcqs.why: The Cl- ion from HCl is common to NaCl, so the equilibrium NaCl(s) (reversible) Na+ + Cl- shifts backwards and pure NaCl precipitates, leaving soluble impurities in solution.

mcqs.q: In the purification of NaCl by passing HCl gas, the common ion is:
mcqs.why: HCl supplies Cl- ions, which are common to the salt NaCl; the increased Cl- concentration forces the equilibrium back towards solid NaCl.

mcqs.q: In the purification of NaCl, the soluble impurities:
options: Stay in solution while pure NaCl precipitates
mcqs.why: Common ion effect is used to purify substances by precipitation: only the NaCl is forced out by the common Cl- ion, leaving the soluble impurities behind in solution.

mcqs.q: The common ion effect is an application of:
mcqs.why: Adding a common ion is a stress on the ionisation equilibrium, and the equilibrium shifts to reduce the stress, exactly as Le-Chatelier's principle describes.

mcqs.q: Adding NH4Cl to NH4OH solution decreases:
options: The ionisation of NH4OH and so the concentration of OH- ions produced by it
The value of Ksp of NH4Cl
mcqs.why: The equilibrium NH4OH (reversible) NH4+ + OH- shifts backwards, so fewer NH4OH molecules ionise and the OH- concentration from the weak base falls.

mcqs.q: The common ion effect generally decreases the:
options: Solubility or ionisation of the weak electrolyte or sparingly soluble salt
mcqs.why: In every example of this lesson, NH4OH, H2S and calcium oxalate, adding the common ion suppresses ionisation and so decreases solubility or the degree of ionisation.

lessons.title: Acidic, Basic and Amphoteric Substances
lessons.notes_html:
Acids turn blue litmus red and liberate H+ ions; they do not have a high pH. Bases turn red litmus blue. Some substances can act as either an acid or a base: they are amphoteric.

Amphoteric Substances

Amphoteric means able to act as either an acid or a base. Water is amphoteric: it donates a proton to NH3 and accepts a proton from HCl. Other examples are the hydrogen carbonate ion HCO3-, which can lose a proton to give CO3^2- or gain one to give H2CO3, and zinc oxide ZnO, which reacts with both acids and bases.

Water as a Weak Acid and a Weak Base

Water donates a proton to a strong base, acting as a weak acid (H2O + NH3 (reversible) NH4+ + OH-), and it accepts a proton from a strong acid, acting as a weak base (H2O + HCl (reversible) H3O+ + Cl-). Its self-ionisation, 2H2O (reversible) H3O+ + OH-, shows both roles at once, and its Kw of 1 x 10^-14 shows both tendencies are very small.

Levelling Effect

The levelling effect is that in water, all acids stronger than H3O+ appear equally strong, and all bases stronger than OH- appear equally strong, because water converts them fully into H3O+ or OH-. For example, HCl, HBr and HClO4 all ionise completely in water, so their relative strengths cannot be distinguished in aqueous solution; a solvent like acetic acid is needed to tell them apart.

pH of Common Substances

Common substances in order of increasing pH are: lemon (about 2), carbonated drink (about 3), apple (about 3.5), tomato (about 4), banana (about 5), potatoes (about 6), milk (about 6.5), water (7), shampoo (about 8), eggs (about 8). Exact values vary with variety and brand, but the order from most acidic to most basic stays the same.

options: Acids turn blue litmus red, and bases turn red litmus blue
Litmus does not change with acids
mcqs.why: Acids turn blue litmus red and liberate H+ ions; they do not have a high pH. Bases turn red litmus blue.

Can act as either an acid or a base

All acids stronger than H3O+ appear equally strong, and all bases stronger than OH- appear equally strong

They do not react with water

mcqs.why: In order of increasing pH: lemon (about 2), carbonated drink (about 3), apple (about 3.5), tomato (about 4), banana (about 5), potatoes (about 6), milk (about 6.5), water (7), shampoo and eggs (about 8).

mcqs.why: Milk has a pH of about 6.5, slightly acidic, just below neutral water (7) in the list of common substances given in this lesson.

lessons.title: The Bronsted-Lowry Theory of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
The Bronsted-Lowry theory defines acids and bases by proton transfer, which works for reactions in water and in other solvents.

Definitions

A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. For example, in HCl + NH3 (reversible) NH4+ + Cl-, HCl donates a proton so it is the acid, and NH3 accepts it so it is the base. In CH3COOH + H2O (reversible) CH3COO- + H3O+, acetic acid is the acid and water is the base.

Conjugate Pairs in Equations

(i) Acetic acid and water: CH3COOH + H2O (reversible) CH3COO- + H3O+. Conjugate pairs: CH3COOH / CH3COO- and H3O+ / H2O. (ii) Ammonia and hydrochloric acid: NH3 + HCl (reversible) NH4+ + Cl-. Conjugate pairs: NH4+ / NH3 and HCl / Cl-. In each pair the two members differ by one proton.

mcqs.q: In the Bronsted-Lowry theory, an acid is a:
mcqs.why: The Bronsted-Lowry theory defines acids and bases by proton transfer: a Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor.

options: NH3 is the acid, HCl is the base
HCl is the acid (proton donor) and NH3 is the base (proton acceptor)
mcqs.why: HCl donates a proton so it is the acid, and NH3 accepts it so it is the base; the products NH4+ and Cl- are their conjugate partners.

options: Acetic acid is the acid and water is the base
Acetic acid is the base and water is the acid
mcqs.why: Acetic acid donates a proton to water, so acetic acid is the Bronsted acid and water is the Bronsted base in this reaction.

mcqs.q: The two members of a conjugate acid-base pair differ by:
mcqs.why: In each conjugate pair the two members differ by one proton: CH3COOH / CH3COO- and H3O+ / H2O in the acetic acid reaction.

mcqs.q: The conjugate pairs in CH3COOH + H2O (reversible) CH3COO- + H3O+ are:
mcqs.why: Each pair differs by one proton: CH3COOH loses a proton to become CH3COO-, and H2O gains a proton to become H3O+, giving the pairs CH3COOH / CH3COO- and H3O+ / H2O.

mcqs.q: The conjugate pairs in NH3 + HCl (reversible) NH4+ + Cl- are:
mcqs.why: NH4+ and NH3 differ by one proton, and HCl and Cl- differ by one proton, so the conjugate pairs are NH4+ / NH3 and HCl / Cl-.

mcqs.q: The Bronsted-Lowry theory works for:
options: Reactions in water and in other solvents, because it is based on proton transfer
mcqs.why: The Bronsted-Lowry theory defines acids and bases by proton transfer, which works for reactions in water and in other solvents.

mcqs.q: In the reaction NH3 + HCl -> NH4+ + Cl-, the conjugate acid of NH3 is:
mcqs.why: NH3 accepts a proton and becomes NH4+; a base that has gained a proton is the conjugate acid, so NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3.

mcqs.q: In CH3COOH + H2O (reversible) CH3COO- + H3O+, the conjugate base of acetic acid is:
mcqs.why: When acetic acid loses its proton it becomes CH3COO-, which is its conjugate base; the pair is CH3COOH / CH3COO-.

mcqs.q: When a Bronsted acid donates a proton, it becomes:
mcqs.why: A conjugate acid-base pair is an acid and a base differing by exactly one proton: when an acid loses a proton it becomes its conjugate base, and when a base gains a proton it becomes its conjugate acid.

lessons.title: Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
lessons.notes_html:
A conjugate acid-base pair is an acid and a base that differ by exactly one proton. When an acid loses a proton it becomes its conjugate base; when a base gains a proton it becomes its conjugate acid.

Conjugate Bases of Given Acids

The conjugate bases are: HClO4 gives ClO4-, HCN gives CN-, H2CO3 gives HCO3-, NH4+ gives NH3. Cl- is the conjugate base of HCl.

Strong Acid, Weak Conjugate Base

The conjugate base of a strong acid is a weak base and the conjugate acid of a strong base is a weak acid. A strong acid ionises completely, so its conjugate base has almost no tendency to accept a proton again, making it a very weak base; for example Cl- from HCl. A strong base likewise takes a proton completely, so its conjugate acid has almost no tendency to lose a proton again, making it a very weak acid. Strength on one side of a conjugate pair always means weakness on the other. So Cl- is a base, though a very weak one.

Classifying Substances as Acids and Bases

BF3 is a Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor); NH3 is a Lewis base (electron-pair donor); NH4+ is a Bronsted acid (proton donor); Ag+ is a Lewis acid; CaO is a base; KCN gives CN-, a base; H2S is an acid; SO4^2- is a base; Na+ is neutral; Cl- is a weak base.
