lessons.title: Strengths of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
Acid and base strength is measured by the ionisation constants Ka and Kb. A large Ka means a strong acid; a small Ka means a weak acid.

Ka, Kb, pKa, pKb

pH = -log[H+], the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration. pOH = -log[OH-], the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration. pKa = -log Ka, measuring acid strength: a smaller pKa means a stronger acid, and a solution with a pKa value of 9 is a weak acid. pKb = -log Kb, measuring base strength: a smaller pKb means a stronger base. A very large Ka value means that the substance is a strong acid.

Ka x Kb = Kw

For a conjugate acid-base pair, Ka x Kb = Kw. The acid constant measures proton loss and the base constant measures proton gain by the conjugate base, and multiplying the two equilibrium expressions cancels to give the ionisation of water, Kw = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C. Taking negative logarithms gives pKa + pKb = pKw = 14. The sum is always 14 because the two constants describe the same proton-transfer equilibrium from opposite sides, and their product is fixed by the ionisation of water. For NH3 and its conjugate acid NH4+: NH4+ (reversible) NH3 + H+, Ka = [NH3][H+] / [NH4+]; NH3 + H2O (reversible) NH4+ + OH-, Kb = [NH4+][OH-] / [NH3]; multiplying gives Ka x Kb = [H+][OH-] = Kw = 1 x 10^-14.

Ionisation Constant of Water

Water ionises as 2H2O (reversible) H3O+ + OH-, with Kw = [H3O+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C. The unit of Kw is mol^2 dm^-6. In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = sqrt(Kw) = 1 x 10^-7 mol/dm^3, so pH = 7 and pOH = 7. In any aqueous medium, pH + pOH = 14, so knowing Kw lets us calculate one from the other. A solution with pH 9 has pOH 5. A solution with [H+] of 10^-3 mol/dm^3 has pH 3. 1 M HCl has zero pH, because pH = -log(1) = 0.

Strongest Halogen Acid

Among the halogen acids HF, HCl, HBr and HI, HI is the strongest acid. HF is the weakest, and its exceptionally low acidic strength is due to strong hydrogen bonding.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: What is the pH of 0.0001 M Ca(OH)2 solution? Solution: Step 1: [OH-] = 2 x 0.0001 = 2 x 10^-4 mol/dm^3. Step 2: pOH = -log(2 x 10^-4) = 3.70. Step 3: pH = 14 - 3.70 = 10.30. Answer: pH = 10.3, as printed in the book.

Numerical 2: What is the [H+] and [OH-] concentration of a solution which has a pH of 4.87? Solution: Step 1: [H+] = 10^-pH = 10^-4.87 = 1.35 x 10^-5 mol/dm^3. Step 2: [OH-] = Kw / [H+] = 1 x 10^-14 / 1.35 x 10^-5 = 7.41 x 10^-10 mol/dm^3. Answers: [H+] = 1.35 x 10^-5, [OH-] = 7.41 x 10^-10 (the book's printed exponent for [OH-] reads 10^-8 in the scan, which does not follow from its own [H+] value; the worked value is 10^-10).

Numerical 3: What is the pH of a 1.0 x 10^-4 M KOH solution? Solution: Step 1: [OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-4 mol/dm^3. Step 2: pOH = -log(1.0 x 10^-4) = 4. Step 3: pH = 14 - 4 = 10. Answer: pH = 10, as printed in the book.

Numerical 4: What is the pH of a solution if the [H3O+] is 6.7 x 10^-4 M? Solution: Step 1: pH = -log[H3O+] = -log(6.7 x 10^-4). Step 2: pH = 3.17. Answer: pH = 3.17, as printed in the book.

Numerical 5: What is the pH of a solution for which [OH-] is 0.15 M? Solution: Step 1: pOH = -log[OH-] = -log(0.15) = 0.82. Step 2: pH = 14 - 0.82 = 13.18. Answer: pH = 13.2, as printed in the book.

lessons.title: Lewis Definition of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
The Lewis definition is wider than the Bronsted-Lowry definition: it uses electron pairs, not protons, so it covers reactions in which no proton is transferred at all.

Definitions

A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. AlCl3 and BF3 are Lewis acids because they have incomplete octets and vacant orbitals that can accept an electron pair. Cl- and NH3 are Lewis bases because they have lone pairs of electrons that they can donate to form a coordinate bond. The classification follows the electron-pair definition, not proton transfer.

NH3 as a Lewis Base

Ammonia has a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen, which it can donate to an electron-pair acceptor to form a coordinate bond, for example NH3 + H+ -> NH4+ and NH3 + BF3 -> H3N-BF3. Donating an electron pair is the Lewis definition of a base, so NH3 is a Lewis base.

Classifying as Lewis Acid or Lewis Base

CO2 is a Lewis acid, H2O a Lewis base, SO2 a Lewis acid, I- a Lewis base, NH3 a Lewis base, OH- a Lewis base, BCl3 a Lewis acid.

lessons.title: Buffer Solutions and their Applications
lessons.notes_html:
A buffer solution resists changes in pH when small amounts of strong acid or base are added. Blood, laboratory preparations and many industrial processes all depend on buffers.

Definition and Buffer Action

A buffer solution is a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of strong acid or base are added. Buffer action works because the buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) in equilibrium. An acidic buffer can be prepared by mixing a weak acid and its salt with a strong base; the example in the book is NH4OH / NH4Cl, a weak base with its salt. In an acetic acid / acetate buffer, added H+ is removed by CH3COO- + H+ -> CH3COOH, and added OH- is removed by CH3COOH + OH- -> CH3COO- + H2O, so the pH stays almost constant.

Why a Buffer Resists pH Change

A buffer resists pH change because it contains both members of a conjugate pair. Added acid is consumed by the basic member and added base by the acidic member, converting the strong acid or base into a weak acid or base that barely changes the hydrogen ion concentration. Only when one member is used up does the pH change sharply.

Applications of Buffer Solutions

Buffer solutions are used to keep the pH of blood constant at about 7.4, in biochemical and pharmaceutical preparations, in electroplating baths, in photography, in leather tanning, and in agriculture to control soil pH. Any process that needs a steady pH uses a buffer.

Buffer Project

Make a buffer solution in the laboratory, for example acetic acid with sodium acetate, and record its pH. Add a small amount of strong acid and record the pH again; it changes very little. Add a small amount of strong base to a fresh sample and record the pH; again it changes very little. The buffer's conjugate pair consumes the added H+ or OH-, keeping the pH nearly constant.

lessons.title: Salts, their Types and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
When a salt dissolves in water, its ions may react with water. That reaction, salt hydrolysis, decides whether the solution is acidic, basic or neutral.

Salt Hydrolysis

Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of the ions of a salt with water to give an acidic or basic solution. Sodium acetate hydrolyses: CH3COO- + H2O (reversible) CH3COOH + OH-, producing hydroxide ions, so the solution is basic. Ammonium chloride hydrolyses: NH4+ + H2O (reversible) NH4OH + H+, producing hydrogen ions, so the solution is acidic. The anion of a weak acid gives a basic solution and the cation of a weak base gives an acidic solution.

Four Types of Salts

Weak acid + strong baseCH3COONaBasic, pH above 7
Strong acid + weak baseNH4ClAcidic, pH about 6
Weak acid + weak baseCH3COONH4pH depends on Ka or Kb

A salt of a weak base and a strong acid has a pH of approximately 6. A 1 M solution of Ca(OH)2 mixed with a 1 M solution of HCl gives a basic product solution, because Ca(OH)2 supplies two OH- ions per formula unit.

lessons.title: Chemical Kinetics
lessons.notes_html:
Chemical kinetics is the study of the rates of chemical reactions and the factors that affect them. It answers how fast a reaction goes, not whether it can go.

Rate of the Reaction

Rate of the reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, in mol dm^-3 s^-1. For the reaction 2N2O5(g) -> 4NO2(g) + O2(g), the rate is (1/2) x rate of disappearance of N2O5 = (1/4) x rate of appearance of NO2 = rate of appearance of O2.

Rate Constant

Rate constant (k) is the proportionality constant in the rate equation; it equals the rate when all reactant concentrations are 1 mol/dm^3, and it depends on temperature. One mole of a reactant reacts with a rate of 0.6 mol dm^-3 s^-1 when the rate constant is 0.6 s^-1 for a first-order reaction.

Order of the Reaction

Order of the reaction is the sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the rate equation, found by experiment. Overall order is the sum of the powers in the rate equation: (a) rate = k[NO]^2[O2] has order 2 + 1 = 3, third order; (b) rate = k[NO]^2 has order 2, second order. A reaction that is first order with respect to A and second order with respect to B has the rate equation rate = k[A][B]^2. For a reaction A -> Product, if doubling the concentration of A quadruples the rate, the reaction is second order.

Rate Law (Rate Equation)

Rate law (rate equation) is the equation relating the rate to the molar concentrations of reactants raised to experimentally determined powers, for example rate = k[A][B].

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: The conversion of X to Y follows second order kinetics. If concentration of X is increased 3 times, to what factor will the rate of formation of Y be increased? Solution: Step 1: For second-order kinetics, rate is proportional to [X]^2. Step 2: Increasing [X] by 3 times multiplies the rate by 3^2 = 9. Answer: 9 times, as printed in the book.

Numerical 2: A first order reaction (A -> Product) has a rate of 0.008 M s^-1 with [A] = 0.002 M. What is the rate constant for this reaction? Solution: Step 1: For a first-order reaction, rate = k[A]. Step 2: k = rate / [A] = 0.008 / 0.002 = 4 s^-1. Answer: 4 s^-1, as printed in the book.

Numerical 3: The decomposition of N2O5 proceeds as 2N2O5(g) -> 4NO2(g) + O2(g). If the rate of decomposition of N2O5 at a particular instant is 4.2 x 10^-7 M s^-1, what is the rate of appearance of (a) NO2 (b) O2? Solution: Step 1: From the equation, the rate is (1/2) x rate of disappearance of N2O5 = (1/4) x rate of appearance of NO2 = rate of appearance of O2. Step 2: Rate of appearance of NO2 = 2 x 4.2 x 10^-7 = 8.4 x 10^-7 M s^-1. Step 3: Rate of appearance of O2 = (1/2) x 4.2 x 10^-7 = 2.1 x 10^-7 M s^-1. Answers as printed in the book.

lessons.title: Rate of Reaction
lessons.notes_html:
The rate of a reaction generally increases when the concentration of a reactant increases, because more reactant particles mean more collisions per second. The exact relation is given by the rate law.

Effect of Concentration

For a first-order reaction doubling the concentration doubles the rate, and for a second-order reaction doubling the concentration quadruples the rate. If the order in a reactant is zero, changing its concentration does not change the rate. Doubling the pressure of a gas doubles the concentrations of both gases, so collisions become more frequent and the rate increases; for a reaction first order in each gas the rate would increase four times. Doubling the number of molecules of gas A doubles its concentration, so the rate increases in proportion to the order in A. You can speed up a reaction by using a more concentrated solution.

Factors that Increase the Rate

The four factors are the nature of the reactants, the concentration of the reactants, the temperature, and the presence of a catalyst. For solid reactants, the particle size (surface area) is a fifth factor: 1 g of aluminium powder reacts most rapidly with 1 M CuSO4 solution, faster than a rod, pellets or ribbon of the same mass, because the powder has the largest surface area. The rate of reaction increases with an increase in temperature and an increase in concentration of reactants.

Worked Numerical

Numerical: The rate constant for the reaction CO + NO2 -> CO2 + NO at 400 degrees C is 0.50 dm^3 mol^-1 s^-1, and the reaction is first order with respect to both CO and NO2. lessons.title: Collision Theory, Transition State and Activation Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Collision theory explains reaction rates from the collisions between reactant molecules. Only a small fraction of collisions actually cause a reaction.

Collision Theory

Collision theory says a reaction occurs when molecules collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation. Most collisions are not effective because the molecules may collide with too little energy to reach the activation energy, or they may collide in the wrong orientation, so the bonds that must break are not struck. Only collisions that are both energetic enough and correctly oriented form the activated complex and lead to products. All collisions between reactant molecules do not lead to reaction for exactly these two reasons.

Activation Energy and Activated Complex

Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that reactant molecules must gain to form the activated complex and react. It acts as an energy barrier: only molecules with energy equal to or above it can react, so the size of the barrier decides how fast a reaction goes. The energy needed to start the reaction is called the activation energy. The activated complex is a substance which is unstable: it cannot be isolated and cannot exist as a product. A collision causes a reaction only if the molecules collide with enough kinetic energy to break old bonds and form the activated complex, that is, energy equal to or greater than the activation energy; slow molecules simply bounce apart unchanged, however often they collide.

Effect of Temperature

With the increase in temperature the rate of reaction increases because more molecules attain the activation energy. Raising the temperature increases molecular speeds, so collisions are more frequent, and more importantly a much larger fraction of molecules now has energy above the activation energy, so the number of effective collisions rises sharply and the rate increases. Increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction by increasing the frequency of effective collisions between reacting molecules. Decreasing the temperature by 10 degrees C lowers the fraction of molecules with activation energy, so the rate falls, roughly to half for many reactions. As the number of effective collisions between the reacting particles increases, the rate of reaction increases.

Methane and Oxygen

Household gas (methane) burns in the presence of oxygen and gives energy for daily use. If a mixture of methane and oxygen is kept in a container for an indefinite period, no reaction takes place, because the molecules do not have enough energy to cross the activation energy barrier, even though the reaction would release energy. A spark or flame supplies the activation energy to a few molecules, and the heat released then activates more molecules, so the burning continues by itself.

Reaction Energy Diagrams

The reaction energy diagram (reaction profile) plots potential energy against the progress of the reaction. For an exothermic reaction the products lie lower than the reactants, delta H is negative, and the peak between them is the activated complex, whose height above the reactants is the activation energy. For an endothermic reaction the products lie higher than the reactants, delta H is positive, and the peak is again the activated complex. In both diagrams the positions to mark are: (a) energy of reactants, (b) energy of products, (c) activation energy, (d) delta H of the reaction.

lessons.title: Catalysis
lessons.notes_html:
A catalyst is a substance that changes the rate of a reaction without itself being consumed. It works by opening a new reaction path with a lower energy barrier.

How a Catalyst Increases the Rate

A catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative reaction path with a lower activation energy, so more molecules can cross the barrier at the same temperature. A catalyst decreases the activation energy and increases the rate of reaction. On a potential energy diagram the catalysed path rises to a lower peak (lower activated complex) than the uncatalysed path, while the energies of reactants and products, and therefore delta H, stay the same. The catalyst is regenerated at the end and is not consumed.

Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Catalysis

When the catalyst and reactants are in different physical phases, the catalysis is called heterogeneous. When they are in the same phase, it is homogeneous.

Hydrogen Peroxide Project

Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to produce oxygen and water: 2H2O2(aq) -> 2H2O(l) + O2(g). The reaction is quite slow unless catalysed by substances such as iodide ions, manganese dioxide or ferric ions. Take a test tube, add about 10 to 15 cm^3 of hydrogen peroxide and add a few crystals of potassium iodide: oxygen bubbles come out rapidly because the iodide catalyses the decomposition. Bring a glowing match stick to the mouth of the test tube: it bursts back into flame, because oxygen supports combustion. Without the catalyst the same reaction is very slow, and the catalyst is not consumed.

lessons.title: General Properties of Solution
lessons.notes_html:
A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The substance present in larger amount is the solvent and the one in smaller amount is the solute. In an atmospheric gaseous solution, nitrogen is the solvent; in ice cream, sugar is the solute.

True Solution, Colloid and Suspension

A true solution has solute particles smaller than 1 nm, invisible even under a microscope, which do not settle, pass through filter paper, and do not show the Tyndall effect. A coarse suspension has particles larger than 1000 nm, visible to the eye, which settle on standing, are caught by filter paper, and scatter light. A colloid lies between the two, with particles of 1 to 1000 nm that show the Tyndall effect but do not settle. Fog is an example of a colloid.

Solubility and its Factors

Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature to form a saturated solution. It depends on the nature of the solute and solvent (like dissolves like), on temperature (most solids dissolve more in hot solvent, gases dissolve less), and on pressure for gases (Henry's law: higher pressure dissolves more gas). Methane (CH4) would not form a solution if added to water, while KCl, HCl and NH3 all dissolve. Phenol and water form a partially miscible liquids system.

Hydration

The process in which water molecules surround and interact with solute ions or molecules is called hydration. The change in enthalpy on dissolving, delta H(sol), the heat of solution, may be positive or negative.

lessons.title: Concentration Units
lessons.notes_html:
The concentration of a solution can be expressed in several units. Some depend on temperature and some do not.

Molarity and Molality

Molarity is moles of solute per volume of solution in dm^3. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Molarity depends on temperature because it is moles per volume of solution, and the volume of a solution expands or contracts with temperature. Molality is moles per kilogram of solvent, and since mass does not change with temperature, molality is independent of temperature. The molarity of pure water in itself is 55.6 mol/dm^3.

ppm, ppb, ppt and Mole Fraction

ppm (parts per million) is the number of parts of solute per million parts of solution, by mass or volume. ppb is parts per billion, and ppt is parts per trillion, used for very dilute solutions. Mole fraction of a component is its moles divided by the total moles of all components in the solution, and it has no units.

Sum of Mole Fractions

For a solution of two components A and B, mole fraction of A is XA = nA / (nA + nB) and of B is XB = nB / (nA + nB). Adding them gives XA + XB = (nA + nB) / (nA + nB) = 1. The same holds for any number of components: the sum of all mole fractions is always one.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Calculate the molarity (M) of: (i) 2.0 g of H2SO4 / 2 dm^3 of aqueous solution (ii) 0.4 g of NaOH / 100 cm^3 of aqueous solution (iii) 0.5 g of Na2CO3 / 250 cm^3 of aqueous solution. Solution: Step 1: (i) Moles of H2SO4 = 2.0 / 98 = 0.0204 mol, volume = 2 dm^3, so M = 0.0204 / 2 = 0.01 M. Step 2: (ii) Moles of NaOH = 0.4 / 40 = 0.01 mol, volume = 100 cm^3 = 0.1 dm^3, so M = 0.01 / 0.1 = 0.1 M. Step 3: (iii) Moles of Na2CO3 = 0.5 / 106 = 0.00472 mol, volume = 250 cm^3 = 0.25 dm^3, so M = 0.00472 / 0.25 = 0.02 M (rounded). Answers as printed in the book: (0.01 M, 0.1 M, 0.02 M).

Numerical 2: Calculate the mole fraction of each component in: (i) 2.5 moles of water (H2O) + 1.5 moles of NaCl (ii) 500 g of water (H2O) + 600 g of glucose (C6H12O6) (iii) 800 g of water (H2O) + 120 g of acetone (CH3)2CO. Solution: Step 1: (i) X(water) = 2.5 / (2.5 + 1.5) = 0.625, X(NaCl) = 1.5 / 4.0 = 0.375. Step 2: (ii) Moles of water = 500 / 18 = 27.78, moles of glucose = 600 / 180 = 3.33, total = 31.11, so X(water) = 0.89, X(glucose) = 0.11. Step 3: (iii) Moles of water = 800 / 18 = 44.44, moles of acetone = 120 / 58 = 2.07, total = 46.51, so X(water) = 0.955, X(acetone) = 0.044. Answers as printed in the book.

Numerical 3: A 3.0 cm^3 cylinder contains a mixture of oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine gases in amounts 4.64 x 10^-5 g, 3.5 x 10^-4 g and 2.3 x 10^-5 g respectively. Calculate the concentration of each in (i) parts per million (ppm) (ii) parts per billion (ppb). Solution: Step 1: (i) ppm: O2 = (4.64 x 10^-5 / 3.0) x 10^6 = 15.46, N2 = (3.5 x 10^-4 / 3.0) x 10^6 = 116.6, Cl2 = (2.3 x 10^-5 / 3.0) x 10^6 = 7.7. Step 2: (ii) ppb = ppm x 1000: O2 = 1.546 x 10^4, N2 = 1.16 x 10^5, Cl2 = 7.7 x 10^3. Answers as printed in the book.

lessons.title: Raoult's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Raoult's law describes how a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of a solvent. The lowering depends only on the number of solute particles, not on what they are.

Statement of Raoult's Law

Raoult's law states that the vapour pressure of a solution equals the mole fraction of the solvent times the vapour pressure of the pure solvent: P = X(solvent) x P0. For a dilute solution the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute.

Lowering of Vapour Pressure

When a non-volatile solute is added, some solvent molecules at the surface are replaced by solute particles, so fewer solvent molecules escape into the vapour, and the vapour pressure of the solution is lower than that of the pure solvent. The relative lowering equals the mole fraction of the solute.

mcqs.why: Raoult's law states that the vapour pressure of a solution equals the mole fraction of the solvent times the vapour pressure of the pure solvent: P = X(solvent) x P0.

Changes the temperature of a solvent

mcqs.why: Raoult's law describes how a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of a solvent; the lowering depends only on the number of solute particles, not on what they are.

options: The mole fraction of the solute
The mole fraction of the solvent
mcqs.why: For a dilute solution the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute, a direct consequence of Raoult's law.

options: Some solvent molecules at the surface are replaced by solute particles, so fewer solvent molecules escape into the vapour

The nature of the solute particles
mcqs.why: Raoult's law describes a colligative-type effect: the lowering depends only on the number of solute particles, not on what they are.

options: P = P0, the vapour pressure of the pure solvent
mcqs.why: With no solute present the mole fraction of the solvent is 1, so P = 1 x P0 = P0; adding solute makes X(solvent) less than 1 and lowers P below P0.

options: Decreases, because the mole fraction of the solvent falls
mcqs.why: More solute means a smaller mole fraction of solvent at the surface, so by Raoult's law P = X(solvent) x P0 falls further below P0.

options: Higher than that of the pure solvent
Lower than that of the pure solvent
Equal to that of the pure solvent
mcqs.why: Because X(solvent) is less than 1 in a solution, P = X(solvent) x P0 is always lower than the vapour pressure P0 of the pure solvent.

mcqs.q: In Raoult's law, P0 stands for:
options: The vapour pressure of the pure solvent
mcqs.why: In P = X(solvent) x P0, P0 is the vapour pressure of the pure solvent and P is the vapour pressure of the solution.

options: The mole fraction of the solute, for a dilute solution
The mole fraction of the solvent
mcqs.why: From Raoult's law, (P0 - P) / P0 = 1 - X(solvent) = X(solute), so for a dilute solution the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute.

lessons.title: Colligative Properties of Solution
lessons.notes_html:
Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not on their nature. The four colligative properties are: lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure.

Elevation of Boiling Point

When a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, the boiling point of the solution is higher than that of the pure solvent, because the vapour pressure is lowered and a higher temperature is needed for it to equal the atmospheric pressure. The elevation is delta Tb = Kb x m, where Kb is the molal elevation constant and m is the molality. The molar mass is M = (Kb x 1000 x w) / (delta Tb x W), where w is the mass of solute and W the mass of solvent in grams.

Depression of Freezing Point

When a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, the freezing point of the solution is lower than that of the pure solvent, because the solute particles hinder the formation of the solid crystal lattice. The depression is delta Tf = Kf x m, where Kf is the molal freezing-point constant and m is the molality. Since m = (1000 x w) / (M x W), the molar mass is M = (Kf x 1000 x w) / (delta Tf x W), where w is the mass of solute and W the mass of solvent in grams. The freezing point of a solution as compared to the solvent is lower.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: In an experiment 6.4 g of an organic compound was dissolved in 25.6 g of benzene and a 1.0 degrees C depression of freezing point was observed. Calculate the molecular weight of the substance (Kf of benzene = 5.12). Solution: Step 1: Molality m = (mass of solute / molar mass) / (mass of solvent in kg) = (6.4 / M) / 0.0256 = 250 / M. Step 2: delta Tf = Kf x m, so 1.0 = 5.12 x 250 / M. Step 3: M = 1280 g/mol. Answer: 1280 g/mol, as printed in the book.

Numerical 2: Calculate the molecular weight of iodine (I2) when a solution containing 1.19 g of I2 in 35.0 grams of ether shows a rise in boiling point by 0.296 degrees C (Kb for ether: 2.22). Solution: Step 1: Molality m = (1.19 / M) / 0.035 = 34 / M. Step 2: delta Tb = Kb x m, so 0.296 = 2.22 x 34 / M. Step 3: M = 255 g/mol, about 254 g/mol as printed in the book (the known molar mass of I2). Answer: molecular weight of I2 = 254 g/mol.

Osmosis

Osmosis is the flow of solvent molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution. The membrane allows solvent molecules to pass but blocks solute particles, so solvent flows until the concentrations equalise or the osmotic pressure balances the flow. A thistle funnel with a membrane and sugar solution rising in its stem demonstrates osmosis. In daily life it explains why potato chips swell in fresh water and shrink in salt solution, why plant roots absorb water from soil, why red blood cells burst in distilled water and shrink in salt solution, and it is used in reverse osmosis plants to desalinate sea water.

Potato Chips Project

Cut equal finger-shaped chips from a potato, measure their lengths, and place three in distilled water and three in concentrated sodium chloride solution. After one hour, take them out and measure again. The chips in distilled water will be longer than before, because water enters the potato cells by endosmosis. The chips in salt solution will be shorter than before, because water leaves the cells by exosmosis into the concentrated solution. Osmosis moves water from a dilute to a concentrated solution across the cell membrane.

A colloid is a mixture in which tiny particles of one substance are dispersed through another. The particles are larger than those in a true solution but too small to settle out.

Classification by Behaviour Towards the Medium

By behaviour towards the medium, colloids are lyophilic (solvent-loving, stable and reversible, like starch in water) or lyophobic (solvent-hating, unstable and irreversible, like gold sol).

Classification by Physical States

By the physical states of the dispersed phase and medium, colloids are sols (solid in liquid), gels (liquid in solid), emulsions (liquid in liquid, like milk), foams (gas in liquid), and aerosols (liquid or solid in gas, like fog and smoke). Fog is an example of a colloid, an aerosol of liquid droplets in air.

lessons.title: Thermodynamics
lessons.notes_html:
Thermodynamics is the study of energy changes in chemical and physical processes. Its first law is the law of conservation of energy.

System, Surroundings and State

The state of a system is its condition described by measurable properties such as pressure, volume, temperature and composition. State functions are properties whose values depend only on the present state of the system, not on how it reached that state, for example pressure, volume, temperature, internal energy, enthalpy and entropy. Heat and work are not state functions because they depend on the path taken. Enthalpy means heat content, and delta H per mole is expressed in units of kJ. Heat is not a state function, while enthalpy, temperature and pressure are.

Internal Energy

The sum of all the energies of all the molecules or atoms of a substance is called its internal energy. The energy possessed by water in a dam is potential energy.

Work and Heat

Work done has a sign: work done by the system on the surroundings (expansion) is negative, and work done on the system by the surroundings (compression) is positive. No work is done at constant volume. Heat capacity depends on the mass of the substance.

lessons.title: Thermochemical Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
A thermochemical reaction is a chemical reaction written with its enthalpy change. The sign of delta H tells whether heat is released or absorbed.

Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions

When heat is absorbed from the surroundings, the process is endothermic. When heat is released to the surroundings, the process is exothermic. Heat of combustion is always negative because burning always releases heat to the surroundings; combustion is always exothermic. Ionisation energy has a positive delta H, while electron affinity and combustion have negative delta H. In the book's exercise, an exothermic reaction is given as the example of a spontaneous reaction.

Enthalpy of Neutralisation

Enthalpy of neutralisation of strong acids and strong bases has always the same value, because neutralisation of any strong acid with any strong base is always the same reaction, H+ + OH- -> H2O, so its enthalpy change is always the same, about -57.3 kJ/mol.

Standard Enthalpy

Standard enthalpy (delta H0) for 1 mole of a substance, which exists in its natural state, at 1 atm pressure is measured at 298 K. Delta H can be measured indirectly by applying Hess's law. 1 kcal is equal to 4.18 x 10^3 J.

Calorimetry

Calorimetry is the measurement of heat changes in chemical or physical processes using a calorimeter, an insulated vessel that prevents heat exchange with the surroundings. To measure an enthalpy change, the reaction is carried out in the calorimeter, the temperature change of the water (and calorimeter) is recorded, and the heat is calculated as q = m x c x delta T, where m is the mass, c the specific heat capacity and delta T the temperature change; at constant pressure this heat equals delta H.

Specific Heat Capacity Project

Weigh an iron bolt and place it in a beaker of water until bolt and water reach the same temperature; record this temperature. Take a dry beaker, weigh it, add 100 mL of water, weigh again to find the mass of water, and heat the water to 70-80 degrees C. Transfer the hot water to a calorimeter, record its temperature T1, then transfer the bolt from the cold water into the calorimeter and record the lowest temperature reached, T2. Heat given out by water is qw = mw x sw x (T1 - T2). The same heat is absorbed by the bolt, so the specific heat of the bolt is sb = qb / (mb x delta T of the bolt). Compare the result with the known specific heat of iron, about 0.45 J/g/K, and discuss heat losses.

lessons.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
lessons.notes_html:
The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another. The total energy of the system and its surroundings remains constant.

Mathematical Form

delta E = q + w, where delta E is the change in internal energy, q is the heat added to the system and w is the work done on the system. Any energy lost by the system is gained by the surroundings, so the total energy of system plus surroundings stays constant.

Pressure-Volume Work

Pressure-volume work is the work done when a system expands or contracts against an external pressure: w = -P delta V. It is related to the first law, delta E = q + w: the change in internal energy of a system equals the heat added to it plus the work done on it. When a gas expands, it does work on the surroundings, so w is negative and the internal energy falls unless heat is supplied.

Heat at Constant Volume and Constant Pressure

The heat of a reaction is the heat absorbed or released when the reaction occurs. At constant volume no pressure-volume work is done, so the heat equals the change in internal energy, qv = delta E. At constant pressure the system may expand or contract, doing work, so the heat equals the change in enthalpy, qp = delta H. The two differ by the work term: delta H = delta E + P delta V = delta E + delta n RT for gases.

Solids and Liquids

Since delta H = delta E + P delta V, and for solids and liquids the volume change delta V is almost zero, the P delta V term vanishes and delta H becomes equal to delta E. Enthalpy change is a state function but heat is not: enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, while heat depends on the path taken (constant pressure or constant volume).

Worked Numerical

Numerical: A chemical reaction takes place in a container of cross sectional area 0.01 m^2, fitted with a weightless and frictionless piston. The piston is moved up through 0.01 m against an external pressure of 101325 Pa as a result of the reaction. Calculate the work done by the system. Solution: Step 1: Work w = P x delta V, and delta V = area x distance moved. Step 2: With the book's printed answer, delta V = 0.001 m^3, so w = 101325 x 0.001 = 101.3 J. Note: the displacement as read in the scan is 0.01 m with area 0.01 m^2, which gives delta V = 1 x 10^-4 m^3 and w = 10.13 J; the book's printed answer 101.3 J corresponds to a displacement of 0.1 m, so the printed distance and the printed answer differ by a factor of ten. Answer as printed in the book: 101.3 J.

lessons.title: Hess's Law: Enthalpy Change Calculations
lessons.notes_html:
Many enthalpy changes cannot be measured directly, because the reaction is too slow, too violent or incomplete. Hess's law lets us calculate them from other measured enthalpy changes.

Hess's Law

Hess's law of constant heat summation states that the total enthalpy change of a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in several steps, because enthalpy is a state function. It follows from the first law of thermodynamics because enthalpy is a state function: the change in a state function depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path. Since energy is conserved, the sum of the enthalpy changes of any set of steps joining the same reactants to the same products must equal the enthalpy change of the direct reaction.

Born-Haber Cycle

The Born-Haber cycle is based on Hess's law: since enthalpy is a state function, the enthalpy change of forming an ionic crystal can be found by adding the enthalpy changes of a cycle of steps (sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron affinity and lattice formation) that start and end at the same states. The cycle is a closed cycle of steps that forms an ionic crystal from its elements: sublimation of the metal, ionisation of the metal atoms, dissociation of the non-metal molecules, electron affinity of the non-metal atoms, and finally lattice formation. By Hess's law the sum of all steps equals the enthalpy of formation of the crystal, so the unknown lattice energy can be calculated from the other known values. For example, using the book's worked values, lattice energy = -405.8 - 88 - 414 - (1/2)(192.5) - (-334.7) = -669.3 kJ/mol.

Ionic Reactions Are Fast

Ionic reactions are very fast because the ions are already free in solution and only need to come together by electrostatic attraction; no covalent bonds have to be broken first.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Apply Hess's law to calculate delta H0 for the sublimation of one mole of iodine from: (i) H2(g) + I2(s) -> 2HI(g), delta H0 = 51.8 kJ/mol (ii) H2(g) + I2(g) -> 2HI(g), delta H0 = -10.5 kJ/mol. Solution: Step 1: Sublimation is I2(s) -> I2(g). Subtract equation (ii) from equation (i): the H2 and HI cancel. Step 2: delta H = 51.8 - (-10.5) = 62.3 kJ/mol. Answer: 62.3 kJ/mol, as printed in the book.

Numerical 2: Calculate the heat of formation of an aqueous solution of NH4Cl from: (i) NH3(g) + aq -> NH3(aq), delta H0 = -35.16 kJ/mol (ii) HCl(g) + aq -> HCl(aq), delta H0 = -72.41 kJ/mol (iii) NH3(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NH4Cl(aq), delta H0 = -51.48 kJ/mol. Solution: Step 1: Add the three steps. Step 2: The sum gives NH3(g) + HCl(g) + aq -> NH4Cl(aq). Step 3: delta H = -35.16 + (-72.41) + (-51.48) = -159.05 kJ/mol (the book prints -159.08 kJ/mol, the difference being rounding of the given values). Answer: about -159.1 kJ/mol.

Numerical 3: Liquid ethanol when burnt in oxygen at 25 degrees C liberates heat, delta H0 = -1402.14 kJ/mol. The heats of formation of CO2 and H2O are -393.50 and -285.81 kJ/mol respectively at the same temperature. Calculate the heat of formation of ethanol at 25 degrees C. Solution: Step 1: Combustion: C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l), delta H = -1402.14 kJ/mol. Step 2: delta H = [2 x (-393.50) + 3 x (-285.81)] - delta Hf(ethanol). Step 3: -1402.14 = -1644.43 - delta Hf(ethanol). Step 4: delta Hf(ethanol) = -1644.43 + 1402.14 = -242.29 kJ/mol (the book prints -242.37 kJ/mol, the difference being rounding). Answer: about -242.3 kJ/mol.

Numerical 4: Determine delta H0 for 2C(s) + 2H2(g) -> C2H4(g) from: (i) C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g), delta H01 = -393.5 kJ/mol (ii) H2(g) + (1/2)O2(g) -> H2O(g), delta H02 = -285.7 kJ/mol (iii) C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), delta H03 = -1430.9 kJ/mol. Solution: Step 1: By Hess's law, delta H = 2 x delta H1 + 2 x delta H2 - delta H3 (twice reaction i, twice reaction ii, minus reaction iii, so that CO2, H2O and O2 cancel). Step 2: delta H = 2 x (-393.5) + 2 x (-285.7) - (-1430.9) = -787 - 571.4 + 1430.9 = 72.5 kJ/mol (the book prints 72.8 kJ/mol, the difference being rounding of the given heats). Answer: about 72.5-72.8 kJ/mol.

options: Enthalpy is a state function: its change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path, and energy is conserved
mcqs.why: Since energy is conserved, the sum of the enthalpy changes of any set of steps joining the same reactants to the same products must equal the enthalpy change of the direct reaction.

mcqs.q: The Born-Haber cycle is based on Hess's law and is used to find:
options: The enthalpy of formation of an ionic crystal, and from it the unknown lattice energy, by adding the enthalpy changes of a cycle of steps
The rate of formation of a crystal
The melting point of a salt
mcqs.why: The cycle adds the steps of sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron affinity and lattice formation; by Hess's law their sum equals the enthalpy of formation of the crystal, so the unknown lattice energy can be calculated.

mcqs.q: Using the book's worked values, the lattice energy from the Born-Haber example is:
Ionic reactions are very fast because:
options: The ions are already free in solution and only need to come together by electrostatic attraction; no covalent bonds have to be broken first
They have low activation energy from catalysts
mcqs.why: Ionic reactions are very fast because the ions are already free in solution and only need to come together by electrostatic attraction; no covalent bonds have to be broken first.

mcqs.q: Given (i) H2 + I2(s) -> 2HI, delta H0 = 51.8 kJ/mol and (ii) H2 + I2(g) -> 2HI, delta H0 = -10.5 kJ/mol, the enthalpy of sublimation of iodine is:
mcqs.why: Sublimation is I2(s) -> I2(g). Subtracting equation (ii) from equation (i), the H2 and HI cancel: delta H = 51.8 - (-10.5) = 62.3 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: From the three steps with delta H0 = -35.16, -72.41 and -51.48 kJ/mol, the heat of formation of an aqueous solution of NH4Cl is about:
mcqs.why: Adding the three steps gives NH3(g) + HCl(g) + aq -> NH4Cl(aq). Adding the enthalpies: -35.16 - 72.41 = -107.57, and -107.57 - 51.48 = -159.05 kJ/mol, about -159.1 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Ethanol burns with delta H0 = -1402.14 kJ/mol, and the heats of formation of CO2 and H2O are -393.50 and -285.81 kJ/mol. The heat of formation of ethanol is about:
mcqs.why: For C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O: products give 2 x (-393.50) = -787.00 and 3 x (-285.81) = -857.43, totalling -1644.43. Then delta Hf(ethanol) = -1644.43 + 1402.14 = -242.29 kJ/mol, about -242.3 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: From the combustion data of this lesson, delta H0 for 2C(s) + 2H2(g) -> C2H4(g) is about:
Hess's law is needed because many enthalpy changes:
options: Cannot be measured directly, because the reaction is too slow, too violent or incomplete
Are too large to write down
mcqs.why: Many enthalpy changes cannot be measured directly, because the reaction is too slow, too violent or incomplete; Hess's law lets us calculate them from other measured enthalpy changes.

lessons.title: Oxidation-Reduction Concepts
lessons.notes_html:
Electrochemistry is the study of the relationship between chemical change and electrical energy. Its foundation is the redox reaction: oxidation and reduction always occur together.

Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the loss of electrons (or increase in oxidation number), for example Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. Reduction is the gain of electrons (or decrease in oxidation number), for example Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. A reduction reaction is one such as Br2 -> 2Br-, while Fe2+ -> Fe3+, Zn -> Zn2+ and Sn2+ -> Sn4+ are oxidations.

Oxidation Number (Oxidation State)

Oxidation state (oxidation number) is the apparent charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic. The oxidation number of Cl in HClO3 is +5. The oxidation number of magnesium in MgCO3 is +2. The oxidation number of Mn is: in KMnO4, +7; in MnO2, +4; in Mn2O7, +7.

Oxidation Numbers of Nitrogen

Step 1: In N2O, 2x + (-2) = 0, so x = +1. Step 2: In NO2, x + 2(-2) = 0, so x = +4. Step 3: In N2O3, 2x + 3(-2) = 0, so x = +3. Step 4: In HNO3, +1 + x + 3(-2) = 0, so x = +5. Step 5: In NH4+, x + 4(+1) = +1, so x = -3. Answers: N2O +1, NO2 +4, N2O3 +3, HNO3 +5, NH4+ -3.

Oxidising and Reducing Agents

Na+ is an oxidising agent because it can accept an electron and be reduced to Na, oxidising another substance in the process. Na metal is a reducing agent because it easily loses its single valence electron to become Na+, reducing another substance. The same element in different oxidation states therefore plays opposite roles.

Balancing by the Oxidation Number Method

Step 1: Find the change in oxidation number: Mn falls from +7 to +2 (gain of 5 electrons), S in H2S rises from -2 to 0 (loss of 2 electrons). Step 2: Balance electrons: 2 Mn atoms gain 10 electrons, 5 S atoms lose 10 electrons. Step 3: Balance the rest by inspection. Balanced equations: (i) 2KMnO4 + 5H2S + 4H2SO4 -> 2KHSO4 + 2MnSO4 + 5S + 8H2O. (ii) 2Fe + 3V2O3 -> Fe2O3 + 6VO. (iii) MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O. (iv) Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. (v) Cu + 2H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O. (vi) 2KMnO4 + 5KNO2 + 3H2SO4 -> 2MnSO4 + 5KNO3 + K2SO4 + 3H2O.

Balancing by the Half-Reaction (Ion-Electron) Method

Balanced equations by the half-reaction method: (i) Sn2+ + 2Fe3+ -> Sn4+ + 2Fe2+ (acidic medium). (ii) 3Zn + Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ -> 3Zn2+ + 2Cr3+ + 7H2O (acidic medium). (iii) 5H2O2 + 2MnO4- + 6H+ -> 2Mn2+ + 5O2 + 8H2O (acidic medium). (iv) Sn2+ + I2 -> Sn4+ + 2I- (neutral). In each case the oxidation half-reaction is multiplied so that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, then H+ and H2O are used to balance oxygen and hydrogen in acidic medium.

lessons.title: Electrode, Electrode Potential and Electrochemical Series
lessons.notes_html:
An electrode is a conductor in contact with an electrolyte. The potential that develops between them is the electrode potential, and comparing electrode potentials predicts which reactions will occur.

Electrode Potential

Electrode potential is the potential difference set up between a metal electrode and the solution of its ions, due to the tendency of the metal to lose electrons or of its ions to gain them. It is measured by connecting the electrode to a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) through a salt bridge and a voltmeter, with all solutions at 1 mol/dm^3 and 25 degrees C; the SHE is assigned 0.00 V and the measured voltage is the electrode's potential. The electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode is chosen as 0 V.

SHE as Anode or Cathode

The standard hydrogen electrode has a reduction potential of 0.00 V, copper has +0.34 V and zinc has -0.76 V. With copper, hydrogen has the lower potential, so it is oxidised and acts as the anode. With zinc, hydrogen has the higher potential, so it is reduced and acts as the cathode. Whether SHE is anode or cathode depends on the other electrode's potential. A cathode has a reduction potential more than the anode.

Zinc, Copper and Aluminium

A zinc rod acts as anode in the Daniell cell but acts as cathode when coupled with an aluminium electrode, because the standard reduction potential of Zn is greater than that of Al. A cell which produces electric current by a redox reaction is called a voltaic cell.

Electrochemical Cells

Electrochemical cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy or vice versa. A voltaic cell has two half-cells joined by a salt bridge: oxidation at the anode releases electrons, which travel through an external wire to the cathode where reduction occurs, producing a current. An electrolytic cell has an external power supply that forces a non-spontaneous reaction, with oxidation at the positive anode and reduction at the negative cathode. Both kinds have two electrodes, an electrolyte, and a complete circuit. A cell in which a non-spontaneous redox reaction is carried out by passing an electric current is an electrolytic cell. In an electrolytic cell the cathode has a negative charge; in a voltaic cell the anode is negative and the cathode is positive.

Reversible and Irreversible Cells

Reversible cells can be reversed by a small opposing current, so their chemical reactions run backwards on charging; the lead storage battery is an example. Irreversible cells cannot be reversed, so once discharged they are discarded; the dry cell is an example.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Given the cells at 25 degrees C, (a) write the cell reactions, (b) calculate the cell voltage: (i) Mg2+/Mg, E0Red = -2.38 V; Cu2+/Cu, E0Red = +0.34 V. (ii) 2H+/H2, E0Red = 0.00 V; Ag+/Ag, E0Red = +0.80 V. Solution: Step 1: (i) Mg/Cu cell: Mg is oxidised at the anode, Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-, and Cu2+ is reduced at the cathode, Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. Cell reaction: Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu. Cell voltage = E(cathode) - E(anode) = 0.34 - (-2.38) = 2.72 V. Step 2: (ii) H2/Ag cell: H2 is oxidised at the anode, H2 -> 2H+ + 2e-, and Ag+ is reduced at the cathode, Ag+ + e- -> Ag. Cell reaction: H2 + 2Ag+ -> 2H+ + 2Ag. Cell voltage = 0.80 - 0.00 = 0.80 V.

Numerical 2: The Daniell cell: at the anode Zn is oxidised, Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, and at the cathode Cu2+ is reduced, Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, giving the cell reaction Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu. Its standard voltage is E0 = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V, and the electrical energy available is W = nFE0 = 2 x 96500 x 1.10 = 212300 J per mole of reaction.

lessons.title: Batteries
lessons.notes_html:
A battery is a voltaic cell, or a set of voltaic cells, that supplies electric current from a chemical reaction. Some batteries can be recharged and some cannot.

Types of Batteries

Batteries are of three main types: primary batteries, which cannot be recharged (dry cell, alkaline cell); secondary batteries, which can be recharged (lead storage battery, nickel-cadmium battery); and fuel cells, which keep working as long as fuel is supplied.

Lead Storage Battery

The lead storage battery is a voltaic cell and it is rechargeable. In the lead storage battery the discharge reactions produce PbSO4 on both plates, and these reactions are reversible. On charging, an external current reverses them, converting PbSO4 back into Pb and PbO2, so the battery can be used again and again. A dry cell cannot be recharged because its reactions are not reversible in this way.

Fuel Cells

A fuel cell, such as the hydrogen-oxygen cell, combines H2 and O2 continuously: at the anode 2H2 + 4OH- -> 4H2O + 4e-, at the cathode O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-, giving water as the only product. Fuel cells are efficient, quiet and pollution-free, and are used in spacecraft and vehicles.

Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws

Electrolysis is the decomposition of an electrolyte by passing an electric current through it. In electrolysis the cations and anions liberated from the electrolyte are discharged. Faraday's first law states that the mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed, m = ZIt. Faraday's second law states that when the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalents (atomic mass divided by valency).

Worked Numerical

Numerical: A certain amount of current is passed through CuSO4 solution for fifty minutes. The net amount of Cu deposited was found to be 25 g. Calculate the current (atomic mass of Cu is 63.5 g). Solution: Step 1: Moles of Cu deposited = 25 / 63.5 = 0.3937 mol. Step 2: Cu2+ needs 2 electrons per atom, so charge = 2 x 0.3937 x 96500 = 76000 C (approx). Step 3: Time = 50 minutes = 3000 s. Step 4: Current I = Q / t = 76000 / 3000 = 25.3 A. Answer: about 25 A. Note: the question's printed phrase about Z = 1 is unclear in the scan; the Faraday calculation above uses the valency 2 of Cu2+.

Electroplating

In electroplating the article to be plated is made the cathode (negative electrode) so that the metal ions in the solution move towards it and are reduced to metal atoms on its surface, forming a smooth coating. If the article were the anode, it would dissolve instead of gaining a coating.

Electrolysis of Water Project

Sharpen two lead pencils at both ends to expose the graphite cores, and fix them vertically about 2 cm apart in a beaker of water acidified with sulphuric acid. Connect one pencil to the positive terminal of a 9 V battery and the other to the negative terminal, and switch on. Bubbles appear at both lower ends: hydrogen at the negative pencil (cathode), 2H+ + 2e- -> H2, and oxygen at the positive pencil (anode), 2H2O -> O2 + 4H+ + 4e-. The pencil joined to the positive pole is the anode and the one joined to the negative pole is the cathode; twice as much hydrogen as oxygen is collected, confirming the electrolysis of water.

Conductors and Non-Conductors

A solution of sugar is a non-conductor but that of table salt is a good conductor of electricity, because sugar dissolves as neutral molecules, which carry no charge, while table salt dissolves as Na+ and Cl- ions, which are free to move and carry current. NaCl is a non-conductor in the solid state but a good conductor in molten form, because in solid NaCl the ions are fixed in the crystal lattice and cannot move, while in molten NaCl the ions become free to move. A weak electrolyte in solution is slightly ionized, while potassium iodide is a strong electrolyte in solution. During electrolysis of fused NaCl, sodium metal is collected at the cathode and not at the anode, because Na+ ions move towards the cathode and gain an electron, Na+ + e- -> Na, while chlorine gas is liberated at the anode.

Nelson Cell

In the Nelson cell for producing NaOH, brine is electrolysed: at the anode 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-, and at the cathode 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-, so the products are chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.
